heading_path: Create your account & generate an API token
chunks.text:
Sign up at vxcloud.io , confirm your email, create your first workspace, and generate a developer API token — the key for every subsequent call.
```
# Workspace setup endpoints are public — no auth required
curl -X POST https://api.vxcloud.io/api/v2/setup/workspace \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "workspace_name": "my-org", "region": "us-east-1" }'

curl -X POST https://api.vxcloud.io/api/v2/setup/api-token \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "token_name": "ci-bot", "expires_in_days": 90 }'
```
- Workspace setup endpoints are public (no auth required).
- The returned token is shown once — store it in a secret manager.
- Pass it on every later request via the X-API-Key header.

chunks.text:
Store cloud credentials encrypted in Vault. AWS , GCP and Azure are supported out of the box and are only decrypted at provisioning time.
```
curl -X POST https://api.vxcloud.io/api/v2/setup/aws-credentials \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "access_key_id": "AKIA...",
    "secret_access_key": "...",
    "region": "us-east-1"
  }'
```
- AWS: access_key_id + secret_access_key + region.
- GCP: project_id + service_account_key JSON.
- Azure: client_id, client_secret, tenant_id, subscription_id.

Call /api/v2/tenant/provision/vm to spin up a VM on any connected cloud. Terraform state, SSH keys and networking are handled for you.
```
curl -X POST https://api.vxcloud.io/api/v2/tenant/provision/vm \
  -H "X-API-Key: vtx_live_your_token" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "provider": "aws",
    "instance_type": "t3.medium",
    "region": "us-east-1",
    "tags": { "env": "production", "team": "platform" }
  }'
```
- Terraform state is managed for you — no local install.
- SSH key pairs are generated and stored in Vault automatically.
- Works across AWS EC2, GCP Compute Engine, and Azure VMs.

Deploy Docker containers, FastAPI apps, React frontends or Kubernetes workloads to that VM with one call. SSH, image pull and process management are handled automatically.
```
curl -X POST https://api.vxcloud.io/api/v2/tenant/container/deploy \
  -H "X-API-Key: vtx_live_your_token" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "image": "nginx:latest",
    "vm_ip": "54.201.10.5",
    "port": 80,
    "env": { "NODE_ENV": "production" }
  }'
```
- Pull from any registry — Docker Hub, ECR, GCR, ACR.
- Environment variables, volume mounts and port mapping supported.
- Stream live logs over /api/v2/tenant/docker/container/ws.

Query resource status, check VM health, stream container logs and track multi-cloud spend in real time through the built-in observability endpoints.

```
# Cost breakdown across every connected cloud
curl -X POST https://api.vxcloud.io/api/v2/tenant/billing/multicloud \

# AI cost-optimization recommendations

```

```
    "workflow": "deploy.yml",
    "ref": "main",
    "inputs": { "env": "production" }

```

heading_path: Register and sync the tenant node
chunks.text:
Open Nodes, select the target node, choose Sync With Workspace, and wait for the health/version checks to finish. For self-hosted workloads the control plane verifies the node identity over HTTPS before binding it to the workspace.

The vxcli command-line interface lets you init projects, plan and deploy infrastructure, manage running services, stream logs, and invoke AI agents — all from your terminal or CI pipeline.
This page documents every command shipped in the binary, grouped by namespace. Each entry ships with multiple runnable examples in a tabbed editor.

Same flow shown as bash, the JSON it returns, and the YAML pipeline you can drop into CI.
```
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Provision a VM, deploy a FastAPI app, watch the service.
set -euo pipefail

vxcli auth login --device

vxcli vm --app api-vm --cloud aws --service ec2 \
  --region us-east-1 --instance-type t3.small \
  --key-pair-name AWSPRODKEY2

vxcli deploy fastapi ./ \
  --host "$(vxcli vm get api-vm --field public_ip)" \
  --ssh-user ubuntu --key-pair-name AWSPRODKEY1.PEM \
  --entry app.app:app --requirements requirements.txt \
  --app-port 8000 --http-port 80 --app-name studio-backend

vxcli services status studio-backend \
  --host "$(vxcli vm get api-vm --field public_ip)" \
  --ssh-user ubuntu --key-pair-name AWSPRODKEY1.PEM
```

chunks.text:
quickstart.sh:
```
# 1. Sign in (exchanges API key → JWT, picks your tenant node)
vxcli auth login -u your-username -k xc_live_…

# 2. Confirm the CLI resolved your tenant node
vxcli node current
# ✓ Active node: node1.vxcloud.io

# 3. Upload your SSH keypair to Vault (stack deploys REQUIRE this — they
#    don't accept --key-pair-location; only --key-pair-name from Vault).
vxcli configure setup vm \
  --key-pair-name AWSPRODKEY1 \
  --pem-file ~/.ssh/aws-prod.pem

# 4. Provision a VM
vxcli vm --app api-vm --cloud aws --service ec2 \
  --region us-east-1 --instance-type t3.small --key-pair-name AWSPRODKEY2

# 5. Make sure your DNS already points at the VM, then deploy with HTTPS
#    (single command — bootstraps Traefik on the VM + ACME via HTTP-01).
vxcli deploy fastapi ./ \
  --host <ip> --ssh-user ubuntu --key-pair-name AWSPRODKEY1 \
  --entry app.app:app --requirements requirements.txt \
  --app-port 8000 --http-port 80 --app-name studio-backend \
  --enable-ssl --domain api.example.com --ssl-email [email protected]

# 6. Manage the running service
vxcli services list   --host <ip> --ssh-user ubuntu --key-pair-name AWSPRODKEY1
vxcli services status studio-backend --host <ip> --ssh-user ubuntu --key-pair-name AWSPRODKEY1
vxcli services restart studio-backend --host <ip> --ssh-user ubuntu --key-pair-name AWSPRODKEY1

# 7. Or drop a single Docker container (HTTPS via host nginx + certbot)
vxcli deploy container grafana \
  --image grafana/grafana:latest \
  --port 3000:3000 \
  --host <ip> --ssh-user ubuntu --key-pair-name AWSPRODKEY1 \
  --enable-ssl --domain grafana.example.com --ssl-email [email protected]

# 8. Open the menu-driven TUI for follow-up
vxcli tui
```

About / version / completion / interactive setup. The minimal commands you’ll run before anything else on a fresh install.
Sign in and inspect your CLI identity. Credentials are stored under ~/.vxcloud/config.json and exchanged for short-lived JWTs against the VxCloud control plane.
Inspect and switch the tenant node the CLI talks to. Each VxCloud workspace is bound to one node (e.g. node1.vxcloud.io); every deploy and install executes there.
Inspect and update the persistent CLI config under ~/.vxcloud/config.json. The interactive `setup` wizard walks first-time users through the same fields.

Provision an application onto a remote VM. The CLI bundles your source (or clones a repo), POSTs it to the tenant node, and the node SSHs into the target VM to build, run, and front the app with nginx (or Traefik in SSL mode). All subcommands share the SSH flag set and the SSL flag set. HTTPS modes — `deploy container --enable-ssl` installs host systemd nginx + certbot in front of the first --port; `deploy <stack> --enable-ssl` (fastapi/react/nextjs/django/golang/...) bootstraps the shared `vxcloud-traefik` container which fronts the docker-compose stack on :443 with a Let's Encrypt cert. Both require the domain's A record to already point at --host. Stack deploys also require the keypair to be uploaded to Vault first (`vxcli configure setup vm --pem-file ./mykey.pem --key-pair-name MYKEY`).

heading_path: Install services from the catalog (vxcli install)
chunks.text: Install a known service from the embedded catalog (Postgres, Grafana, Ollama, Kafka, …) or run a custom install script / docker-compose stack. The catalog ships inside the binary — no repo clone needed.

heading_path: Manage services on remote VMs (vxcli services)
chunks.text: The lifecycle plane: start / stop / restart / status / logs / remove a Docker container, plus host-level ops (reboot, cleanup, diagnostics) under `vxcli services vm`. Sibling to install (which CREATES) and deploy (which DEPLOYS).

heading_path: Sessions & lifecycle (vxcli sessions, apply, pull, delete, status, import)
chunks.text: A deploy/install creates a session — a tracked, replayable, inspectable unit of work. These commands list, replay, fetch, and tear down those sessions.
AI agents for git, DevOps, and infrastructure operations. Tools are deterministic; reasoning is delegated to the model when an LLM is present.

UI parity for /dashboard/?tab=agentcontrol — every action the web dashboard exposes (Models, Datasets, Training, Pipelines, Fine-tuning, Embeddings, Knowledge, Tools, MCP, Evals, Programming, Web Assets, Deployments) is reachable from the CLI. Auto-injects X-Tenant-ID from your JWT; override with `--tenant <id>`. Use `--data/-d <json|@file>` for POST/PUT/PATCH bodies.

Browse and provision marketplace agents (FastAPI agents like prompt_agent / web_scraper_agent / research_deep_agent), models (embedding/retrieval like basic_model_chromadb / basic_model_faiss), and Terraform solutions (turnkey infra modules like terraform_aws_eks_enterprise, terraform_gcp_cloudrun, terraform_azure_three_tier_application). Aliases: `vxcli mp`.

Manage CI/CD pipelines, builds, Git-provider connections, and per-pipeline env vars. Pipelines back onto GitHub Actions (workflow_dispatch), so `trigger` issues a real GitHub workflow run when wired to a GitHub repo.
Run a network diagnostic / security-audit script (DNS, bandwidth, ports, security audit) locally or over SSH on a remote host. The catalog is embedded in the binary.

Ephemeral dev environments — disposable Docker-in-Docker sandboxes you can SSH into, deploy to, then throw away. Useful for trying a deploy script without touching a real cloud VM. Each sandbox is reachable over a per-user nginx proxy.
VxChrono is the per-tenant goal executor + cron scheduler. Define missions (a goal + a model + an optional cron) and the tenant node drives them — single-shot, on-cron, or until-success.

VXCOMPUTER is the per-tenant-node, file-backed agent control plane — policies, audit log, gateway for agent → tool calls. No external DB; everything lives on the node. Use these commands to inspect/configure the runtime before running agents.

Goroutine-powered web crawler, multi-engine search (Google/Yahoo/Bing/DuckDuckGo/Wikipedia/Yellow Pages), and an LLM-orchestrated "deep research" mode that fans seeds out, summarises pages, and produces a single answer. Ships as part of vxcli; backed by the webscraper agent on the tenant node (Ollama is the default LLM provider).
Register robots and fleets, push commands, and stream telemetry. The control plane is multi-tenant; each robot is paired to a tenant by short code or QR.

The SalesShift product surface: tracked email, dashboard stats, the tenant node email worker, and the global prospect pool. Aliases: `vxcli ss`, `vxcli sales`. Auth is whatever `vxcli auth login` stored — an `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>` when an access token is present, otherwise `X-API-Key` — so there is nothing extra to configure. Every leads command honours `--output text|json|yaml`; email, stats and worker always print text. HTTP timeout is 90s. Twenty-one of the entries below are commands; the last three are reference notes covering the shared `--output` flag, exit codes, and what to do when the group is missing. Between them they reach 21 of SalesShift's 363 API operations — deals, sequences, quotes, contracts, invoices, calendar, deliverability and messaging have no command, so use the REST API for those.
AI chat plus the infrastructure namespaces — docker, vm, kubernetes, serverless, storage, network. Each opens further subcommands; this section lists the entry points.
Real failure modes observed in production deploys. Most of these are one-line fixes once you know them — but they're non-obvious and the error messages can mislead.

Every command that SSHes to a target VM accepts either:
- --key-pair-name <name> — the tenant node resolves the SSH key from your workspace Vault. The key never leaves the server.
- --key-pair-location <path> — read a local PEM (e.g. ~/.ssh/id_rsa or ./mykey.pem ) and attach it to the deploy request as private_key_pem . Path resolution honors ~ ; permissions tighter than 0600 are warned. Key is uploaded over TLS.
You must set at least one of the two; passing both keeps the deploy backwards-compatible while the server-side support for private_key_pem rolls out.

heading_path: Authentication: shared across all three SDKs
chunks.text:
Every SDK supports the same auth flow:
- Construct the client with an API key ( xc_dev_* , xc_test_* , or xc_live_* ).
- The first protected call exchanges the key for a JWT against /api/v1/auth/developer/keys/login .
- On 401, a single-flight refresh re-exchanges and retries once.
- Or call .loadFromVxcli() to pick up credentials written by vxcli auth login .
For SSH-bound operations (deploy / install / services / networks), pass either keyPairName (Vault-managed) or keyPairLocation (local PEM, attached as a private_key_pem multipart part).

This page covers what SalesShift is, how it sits on the platform, the bring-your-own-key model, and exactly how much of it vxcli and the SDKs reach. The per-route reference lives in SalesShift’s own docs app.
```
# The credential vxcli already holds works against SalesShift —

vxcli auth login -u your-username -k xc_live_…
```

One credential, one control plane

chunks.text:
SalesShift is a sales-execution product: contacts and companies, deal pipelines, multi-step outbound sequences and one-off campaigns, a global prospect pool with metered reveals, a product catalogue that feeds quotes, quotes that freeze into e-signable contracts, invoices with PDFs and recorded payments, recurring subscriptions with an MRR rollup, a calendar with real ICS invitations and working RSVP, plus team messaging and WebRTC calls.
It is not a separate service you deploy. Its routers live inside the same FastAPI control plane that serves the rest of this documentation, under two prefixes:
- /api/v1/salesshift — 306 operations across 24 router modules.
- /api/v1/messaging — 57 operations: rooms, messages, guest invites and call metadata.
One piece runs off the control plane: the outbound email worker lives on your tenant node and answers at GET {node} /api/v2/salesshift/email/health — the same node vxcli node current reports.

heading_path: It runs on the VxCloud platform
chunks.text:
Same credential. 281 of the 363 routes resolve the caller through the same dependency the rest of the platform uses, and accept either Authorization: Bearer <jwt> or X-API-Key: xc_live_… . Every query is then filtered by the organization that credential resolves to. There is no separate SalesShift key.
Same tooling. vxcli salesshift is a command group in the same binary; the SDK methods hang off the same client object you use to provision a VM. You do not install anything extra.
Same Vault. Provider credentials go to your workspace Vault namespace — the one described in Store and rotate cloud credentials with Vault . Postgres holds only the metadata row.
Same node. The email worker is a service on your tenant node, so send throughput and rate limiting are governed by hardware you already control.
One thing to know first
The running service is constructed with openapi_url=None , so /openapi.json and /docs return 404 on the API host. Do not point a generator at them — use SalesShift’s own docs app instead.

SalesShift sends through providers you connect, not through a platform account you rent capacity from. An organization registers its own mailboxes (IMAP/SMTP, or an OAuth mailbox), its own AI provider and its own enrichment key. You are billed by those providers directly, at their rates.
Payments are the exception. Invoicing is designed around your own Stripe account, but Stripe cannot be connected yet: POST /api/v1/salesshift/settings/integrations answers 400 Unsupported provider: payment/stripe , and Settings → Integrations has no payments group. Invoices, PDFs and manually recorded payments work without it; hosted card checkout does not.

- ▸ POST /api/v1/salesshift/settings/integrations writes the credential into your workspace Vault and upserts a metadata row — provider, active flag, Vault path, last-tested timestamp. The secret itself never lands in Postgres.
- ▸ POST /api/v1/salesshift/settings/integrations/ {id} /test reads the credential back out and uses it against the provider for real. A Vault round-trip on its own proves nothing about whether the key, host, port or password still work.
- ▸ GET /api/v1/salesshift/settings/integrations lists what an organization has connected, by type — email, AI, payment.
Connecting your own provider is optional, not a prerequisite. Sending and the AI assistant both have a managed default, so an organization with no integrations at all still drafts and still sends. Connecting one replaces the managed path for that capability and stops the usage drawing on your allowance — a connected model key spends no AI credits. The test organization here has three integrations and all three are email (imap, smtp, smtp).

The API is the whole product. The CLI and the SDKs are deliberately narrower — they cover email and the leads pool, and nothing else.
363 operations across 27 router modules — CRM, deals, sequences, campaigns, quotes, contracts, invoices, calendar, deliverability, leads, webmail, messaging and calls.
21 commands: tracked email send/list, dashboard stats, the node email worker health check, the leads pool, and saved searches. Nothing else in SalesShift has a command.
20 of the 306 SalesShift routes — the four email/stats calls plus the leads pool. None of the 57 messaging routes.
The CLI has no contact commands. A contact is created by converting a lead — vxcli salesshift leads convert , leads bulk-convert or leads convert-from-pool — because conversion is where consent metadata is written. Nothing else in the CRM is scriptable from the CLI today.

Five languages carry a SalesShift surface. All five expose the same two things: the four email/stats calls and the leads pool — 20 of the 306 SalesShift routes, and none of the 57 messaging routes. Deals, sequences, quotes, contracts, invoices, calendar, deliverability and webmail have no SDK method in any language; reach them over HTTP.
Language
Entry point
Methods
Status
Python
Dicts and lists. Typed exceptions only (VxAuthError, VxValidationError, …).
23 sync · 23 async
Eight methods were called against a running control plane and all eight returned the documented shapes.
TypeScript
The most thoroughly typed of the five — ~30 exported interfaces, overloads on searchLeads, exported caps, named lead errors.
22
Read in full but not built or executed. getStats is the one call with no result interface (Record<string, unknown>).
Go
Typed structs for every request and response, plus MailableEmail(), NeedsReveal(), DisplayTotal() and Describe() helpers.
25
Read in full but not compiled or executed. The routes behind it were exercised directly and through the Python SDK.
C++
Requests are typed (LeadFilters, LeadSearchRequest, LeadUpdate). Every method returns std::string — the raw JSON body.
21
Lives in the SDK tree at sdk/cpp/ and has the same leads surface, but it is not part of this reference and has no response types or paging helper.
Java
Requests use LeadQuery / LeadUpdate builders. Every call returns String — the raw JSON body.
26
Lives at sdk/java/ as a single file with the same leads surface. Four static helpers exist so a caller can explain a failure without parsing the JSON.
All five implement one written contract, so "reveal" costs the same thing and a masked address looks the same everywhere. Two rules matter more than the rest: leads are not mailable until they are converted, and an unrevealed address is a mask, not an address — the Python and Go bindings refuse a masked address on the send path rather than let it reach a real domain.

heading_path: Two things that are built but undemonstrated
chunks.text:
Everything else named on this page was verified working against the live system. These two were not, and it would be dishonest to let a rollout plan assume otherwise.
OAuth mailbox connect has never had a real consent
The flow is fully built — PKCE, tokens in Vault, XOAUTH2, refresh — and a real send completes AUTH XOAUTH2 → 250 queued. But no Microsoft or Google mailbox has ever consented in this deployment, so the final SMTP hop to a real provider is unproven. Affects the webmail OAuth connect, reconnect and callback routes.
Call transcription and summary have never run on real data
No organization here has an AI provider key configured, which is the condition the transcription path checks. Every recording therefore ends at status="unavailable". The recording upload, finalize and intelligence routes are implemented; their AI output is undemonstrated.

vxcli salesshift email send — Send one tracked email. Goes through the same engine sequences use — suppression gate, per-mailbox daily caps, the tenant node worker, open/click tracking. Exits 1 unless the call returns HTTP 200 AND success=true, printing the server's own detail. Not run in the verification pass that produced this page, because it sends a real email. Usage: vxcli salesshift email send --to --subject (--body | --body-file ) Flags: - --to: Recipient address (required) → to_email - --subject: Subject; merge tags like {{first_name}} resolve against the contact record (required) - --body: HTML body (required unless --body-file) - --body-file: Read the HTML body from a file instead. A read error exits 1 before anything is sent. Inline body: ```bash vxcli salesshift email send \ --to ada@acme.com \ --subject "Quick question about your rollout" \ --body '

Hi {{first_name}}, saw you shipped v2 — worth 15 minutes?

' ``` From a file (recommended): ```bash # Keeps quoting out of it, and lets the HTML live in version control. vxcli salesshift email send \ --to ada@acme.com \ --subject "Following up, {{first_name}}" \ --body-file ./templates/followup.html ``` Never send to a pool address: ```bash # A pool row's address is MASKED until you pay to reveal it, and a lead # is not mailable even once revealed — conversion to a Contact is where # consent metadata is written. Both SDK bindings that check refuse a # masked address outright; do the same in your own scripts. # # h•••@deltatre.com <- a mask. Not an address. Never send here. # # The supported route is: vxcli salesshift leads convert-from-pool # -> Contact vxcli salesshift email send --to … ```

chunks.text:
vxcli salesshift leads search — Search the global prospect pool — people by default, companies with --companies. Addresses come back MASKED (j•••@acme.com) unless your organization has already revealed them. The pool is global and the masking decision is made on the control plane; the tenant node never sees it.
Usage: vxcli salesshift leads search [filters] [--sort <field>] [--desc] [--limit 25] [--cursor <c>] [--all] [--companies]
Flags:
- --q: Free text over name, title and company → filters.q
- --title: Title contains (repeatable, OR'd) → filters.titles[]
- --exclude-title: Title must NOT contain (repeatable) → filters.exclude_titles[]
- --seniority: founder | c_suite | vp | director | manager | senior | entry (repeatable)
- --department: engineering | sales | marketing | finance | hr | ops | legal | executive (repeatable)
- --country: ISO-2 country, e.g. AU (repeatable)
- --industry: Industry, e.g. "Computer Software" (repeatable)
- --email-status: verified | unverified | guessed | catch_all | invalid (repeatable)
- --employees: Company size band, e.g. 51-200 (repeatable)
- --domain: Company domain, e.g. canva.com (repeatable)
- --keyword: Company keyword, substring match (repeatable)
- --min-score: Minimum quality score (int, omitted from the body when 0)
- --has-email: Only rows where an address EXISTS — you still have to reveal it. Tri-state: sent only when you actually pass the flag, so omitting it means "no constraint" and `--has-email=false` is a real filter.
- --has-phone: Only rows where a phone number exists. Tri-state, same rule as --has-email.
- --sort: people: score | name | title | company | location | employees | email. companies: score | name | employees | industry | location. Default score.
- --desc: Sort descending. Default is descending for score/employees, ascending for text fields.
- --limit: Rows per page. Clamped client-side to 1..100, and raised to 100 under --all. Default 25.
- --cursor: Opaque cursor from a previous page. Invalid after you change --sort or any filter — a keyset position only means something inside the result set it came from.
- --all: Walk every page. Stops after 200 pages and says so rather than pretending the set is complete.
- --companies: Search companies instead of people.
Targeted search:
```bash
# Repeatable flags are OR'd within a field and AND'd across fields.
vxcli salesshift leads search \
  --country AU --country NZ \
  --seniority founder --seniority c_suite \
  --department executive \
  --employees 51-200 \
  --has-email \
  --limit 25
```
Paging:
```bash
# Page by cursor. Do NOT change --sort or a filter between pages —
# the cursor is a keyset position inside the previous result set.
vxcli salesshift leads search --country AU --limit 100 --output json \
  | jq -r '.next_cursor'

vxcli salesshift leads search --country AU --limit 100 --cursor "<cursor>"

# Or let the CLI walk it. --all raises --limit to 100 and stops at 200
# pages, reporting pages_walked and walk_truncated in the JSON.
vxcli salesshift leads search --country AU --all --output json
```
Companies:
```bash
vxcli salesshift leads search --companies \
  --industry "Computer Software" --employees 201-500 \
  --sort employees --desc --limit 20

# Company results are unpaged server-side — there is no next cursor.
```
Scripting it:
```bash
# Under --output json|yaml the human chatter (cost warnings, prompts)
# goes to stderr, so the parseable stream stays clean.
vxcli salesshift leads search --country AU --limit 100 --output json \
  | jq -r '.items[] | select(.email_revealed == false) | .pool_id' \
  > candidates.txt

# Matches is capped for display at 10,000 — past that it is marked an
# estimate. Don't budget reveals off it.
```
code_blocks:
# Repeatable flags are OR'd within a field and AND'd across fields.
vxcli salesshift leads search \
  --country AU --country NZ \
  --seniority founder --seniority c_suite \
  --department executive \
  --employees 51-200 \
  --has-email \
  --limit 25

# Page by cursor. Do NOT change --sort or a filter between pages —
# the cursor is a keyset position inside the previous result set.
vxcli salesshift leads search --country AU --limit 100 --output json \
  | jq -r '.next_cursor'

vxcli salesshift leads search --country AU --limit 100 --cursor "<cursor>"

# Or let the CLI walk it. --all raises --limit to 100 and stops at 200
# pages, reporting pages_walked and walk_truncated in the JSON.
vxcli salesshift leads search --country AU --all --output json

vxcli salesshift leads search --companies \
  --industry "Computer Software" --employees 201-500 \
  --sort employees --desc --limit 20

# Company results are unpaged server-side — there is no next cursor.

# Under --output json|yaml the human chatter (cost warnings, prompts)
# goes to stderr, so the parseable stream stays clean.
vxcli salesshift leads search --country AU --limit 100 --output json \

# Matches is capped for display at 10,000 — past that it is marked an
# estimate. Don't budget reveals off it.

vxcli salesshift leads quota — Your organization's reveal meter for the current period: used, allowance, remaining. Read-only and free — check it before any bulk reveal or convert-from-pool.
Usage: vxcli salesshift leads quota [--output json|yaml]

vxcli salesshift leads reveal — Un-mask one pool person. SPENDS one reveal from the metered allowance (free if this organization already revealed them). The command fetches the quota first and prints the cost BEFORE the call, then prints the quota again afterwards. Revealing does not make the person mailable — convert first.
Usage: vxcli salesshift leads reveal <pool-id> [--yes]
Flags:
- --yes: Skip the confirmation prompt. Required in CI, where there is no one to answer it.
Example:
```bash
vxcli salesshift leads reveal 36d9e92d-… --yes
# Prints: the cost notice, then Pool ID / Email / Phone / LinkedIn,
# the quota after the spend, and a reminder that a revealed lead is
# still not mailable.
#
# HTTP 402 -> "reveal allowance spent — nothing was charged for this
# attempt." HTTP 410 -> "removed at the person's request" (terminal).
```

chunks.text:
vxcli salesshift leads convert-from-pool — Pool → Contact in one action: save, reveal if needed, convert. SPENDS quota unless you pass --no-reveal. Prints the cost before acting and every bucket afterwards — including the zeros — because rendering only the success count of a partial spend is how people stop believing the meter. Refuses more than 200 ids.
Usage: vxcli salesshift leads convert-from-pool <pool-id> [<pool-id> …] [--no-reveal] [--yes]
Flags:
- --no-reveal: Do not spend quota. Rows whose address is still masked are skipped rather than revealed.
- --yes: Skip the confirmation prompt (required in CI).
Example:
```bash
vxcli salesshift leads convert-from-pool 36d9e92d-… 0d730b59-… --yes
# Requested / Converted / Revealed now / Already converted
# Skipped — no quota / Skipped — no email / Skipped — erased
# Contact IDs (first 10), then the quota after the spend.
#
# Every id lands in exactly one bucket, so the buckets sum to the number
# of ids passed. The CLI warns when they don't.
```

vxcli salesshift leads erasure — Right to be forgotten. Erases a person from the pool for EVERY tenant, not just yours, and flags every tenant's saved copy. Irreversible. The command prints that warning and the subject address before it asks for confirmation.
Usage: vxcli salesshift leads erasure --email <addr> [--reason gdpr_erasure] [--note <text>] [--yes]
Flags:
- --email: The person to erase (required)
- --reason: Recorded reason (default gdpr_erasure)
- --note: Free-text note; omitted from the body when empty
- --yes: Skip the confirmation prompt. Think hard before scripting this one.
Example:
```bash
vxcli salesshift leads erasure --email person@example.com
# ! GLOBAL and IRREVERSIBLE — this removes the person for every tenant.
# Subject: person@example.com
# ? Continue? [y/N]
#
# On success: Pool rows erased / Saved leads flagged / Already recorded.
```

heading_path: Exit codes and the two errors worth branching on
chunks.text:
Exit codes and the two errors worth branching on — The leads commands name failures by HTTP status rather than by matching message text. 402 means the reveal allowance is spent and NOTHING was charged for the attempt. 410 means the record was removed at the person's request — terminal, for every tenant, and retrying will never succeed. 404 and 400 pass the server's own detail through; 400 also names the two usual causes. 401/403 tells you to run `vxcli auth login`. Anything else prints "<action> failed (HTTP <code>)".
Usage: # Branch on the exit, not on the message
Example:
```bash
if ! vxcli salesshift leads reveal "$POOL_ID" --yes; then
  # 402: allowance spent — you were not charged. Stop the batch.
  # 410: erased at the person's request. Skip and never retry.
  echo "reveal failed — see the message above" >&2
fi

# Before logging in at all, the leads commands print
#   'not authorized — run `vxcli auth login`'
# and the stats/email path prints 'stats failed (HTTP 401)'.
```
code_blocks:
if ! vxcli salesshift leads reveal "$POOL_ID" --yes; then
  # 402: allowance spent — you were not charged. Stop the batch.
  # 410: erased at the person's request. Skip and never retry.
  echo "reveal failed — see the message above" >&2
fi

# Before logging in at all, the leads commands print
#   'not authorized — run `vxcli auth login`'
# and the stats/email path prints 'stats failed (HTTP 401)'.

If `vxcli salesshift` says "unknown command" — The command group is newer than some checked-in binaries. A build of the CLI that predates it answers `unknown command "salesshift"` — that is a stale binary, not a missing entitlement. Re-install from the published installer, or rebuild the CLI from source, then re-run.
Usage: vxcli version && vxcli salesshift --help
Example:
```bash
# Re-install and confirm the group is present
curl -fsSL https://vxcloud.io/download/cli/install.sh | sh
vxcli salesshift --help

# Aliases, if you type this a lot:
vxcli ss stats
vxcli sales leads quota
```

chunks.page_title: Send your first tracked email with SalesShi…
chunks.text: Everything here lives in the SalesShift web app. You need two things before the first send: a mailbox connected under Settings, and a contact to send to. A lead is not a contact — that distinction costs people their sending domain, so it is the first thing this guide pins down.

chunks.page_title: Send your first tracked email with SalesShi…
heading_path: Connect a mailbox (this is the BYOK step)
chunks.text:
Open Settings → Integrations. Add an integration of type email — either a plain IMAP/SMTP mailbox (host, port, username, password) or an OAuth mailbox. The credential is written into your workspace Vault; Postgres keeps only the metadata row (provider, active flag, the Vault path, and when it was last tested). Nothing about your password is stored in the database.
- ▸ The integration list is exactly what the org has connected — the same rows GET /api/v1/salesshift/settings/integrations returns, grouped by type: email, AI, payment.
- ▸ Use the per-integration Test action after saving. It reads the credential back out of Vault and uses it against the provider for real. A Vault round-trip on its own proves nothing about whether the host, port or password still work.

chunks.page_title: Send your first tracked email with SalesShi…
heading_path: Check the email worker before you send anything
chunks.text:
Outbound mail does not go out from the control plane — it goes through a Go worker running on your tenant node, the same node vxcli node current reports. Confirm it is up and which providers it has: the health endpoint reports status, the provider list, whether Redis is connected, and the per-domain rate limit in messages per minute.
```
# The one SalesShift call that does not carry a credential — it is a
# plain GET against your own node.
vxcli salesshift worker health

# Node             https://node1.vxcloud.io
# Status           healthy
# Providers        [smtp]
# Redis            true
# Domain rate/min  20
```
code_blocks:
# The one SalesShift call that does not carry a credential — it is a
# plain GET against your own node.
vxcli salesshift worker health

# Node             https://node1.vxcloud.io
# Status           healthy
# Providers        [smtp]
# Redis            true
# Domain rate/min  20

chunks.page_title: Send your first tracked email with SalesShi…
heading_path: Understand what you are allowed to send to
chunks.text:
SalesShift has three kinds of person record and only one of them is mailable.

A pool person is a row in the global prospect pool. Their address comes back masked — j•••@acme.com — until your organization spends a metered reveal on it.

A saved lead is a snapshot of a pool person copied into your org. Still not mailable.

A contact is a CRM record. Converting a lead is what creates one, and conversion is where consent metadata is written. Only a contact address goes into a send.
- ▸ has_email tells you an address exists. email_revealed tells you whether you may see it. They are different questions.
- ▸ The Python and Go bindings refuse a masked address on the send path outright, rather than let it reach a real domain. Do the same in your own scripts.

chunks.page_title: Send your first tracked email with SalesShi…
chunks.text: Open Contacts. Either create one directly, or convert a lead: from Leads → Pool, open a person, reveal them (this spends one from your metered allowance), then convert. Conversion is idempotent — a lead that already has a contact reports the existing contact id rather than creating a second one.

chunks.page_title: Send your first tracked email with SalesShi…
chunks.text:
From the contact record, compose and send. The send goes through the same engine sequences use, in this order: suppression gate → per-mailbox daily cap and warmup ramp → the tenant node worker → tracking pixel and click rewriting → the event stream. A suppressed or unsubscribed recipient is rejected, and that gate is not optional.
- ▸ Merge tags such as {{first_name}} resolve against the contact record, in both the subject and the body.
- ▸ The response names the provider that actually carried the message — node-smtp, smtp, sendgrid, mailgun, platform or sink — plus a tracking id.

chunks.page_title: Send your first tracked email with SalesShi…
chunks.text: Two places show what happened. The email list shows every tracked outbound message with its status, open count and click count. The Conversations view shows the full thread with one contact — every tracked send plus any captured reply. Reply detection runs an IMAP pass roughly every five minutes, so a reply takes a few minutes to appear.

chunks.page_title: Send your first tracked email with SalesShi…
chunks.text:
The dashboard counters roll everything up: contacts, companies, open deals, active sequences, and the email funnel — sent, delivered, opened, replied, bounced. It is the fastest way to confirm your first send actually registered.
Stuck halfway through? Email [email protected] — most replies land within an hour during weekdays.
Was this page helpful?

chunks.page_title: Set up a sending pool and protect deliverab…
chunks.text: Settings → Deliverability is one page with four parts: the pool itself, org-level switches, domain authentication, and inbox placement. Work through them in that order — the placement test is only meaningful once the mailboxes and DNS are right.

chunks.page_title: Set up a sending pool and protect deliverab…
heading_path: Connect every mailbox you intend to send from
chunks.text: The pool is built from the mailboxes your organization has connected — the same ones from Settings → Integrations and Settings → Mail. A pool of one is legitimate and often correct; rotation is for teams sending enough volume that a single mailbox would hit its cap.

chunks.page_title: Set up a sending pool and protect deliverab…
chunks.text:
The pool view lists every connected mailbox with its cap, ramp position, health and — when it is not sending — the reason. Alongside it are the org totals: how many mailboxes are pooled, how many are actually sendable, how many are paused, how many need reconnecting, today's capacity, what is left of it, the org-wide daily ceiling, and which mailbox is up next.
- ▸ The health numbers are the last computed snapshot, not a fresh calculation. The page tells you when they were computed, how old that is, and whether a refresh is running.
- ▸ That is deliberate. Computing health inline would couple page latency to write volume, and a page that times out shows you nothing at all — which is worse than slightly older numbers, as long as it says so.
- ▸ A mailbox that needs reconnecting is counted separately from a paused one, because the fix is different: one needs a new consent, the other needs a decision.

chunks.page_title: Set up a sending pool and protect deliverab…
heading_path: Set a cap and a warmup ramp per mailbox
chunks.text:
Each mailbox carries its own policy: whether it is in the pool, its weight in the rotation, a daily cap, a ramp start date with an initial volume and a daily increment, and a minimum gap between sends. The ramp is the important one for a new mailbox — it starts you low and adds a fixed amount per day instead of letting a cold mailbox send at full cap on day one.
- ▸ The org defaults are shown on the same page, so you can see what a mailbox inherits before you override it.
- ▸ Pause state is deliberately not editable in this policy form. Pausing and resuming have their own actions so that lifting a pause always records who lifted it.

chunks.page_title: Set up a sending pool and protect deliverab…
heading_path: Turn rotation on — as an explicit decision
chunks.text: Rotation ships OFF. Turning it on changes which address your mail comes from, and doing that to a live domain without being asked is a good way to damage a sending reputation. So it is a switch someone flips once, knowingly, after confirming the mailboxes are configured. The same panel sets the health window in days.

chunks.page_title: Set up a sending pool and protect deliverab…
heading_path: Fix domain authentication before you test anything
chunks.text:
The domains view lists every sending domain your mailboxes use, with the last DNS answer for each: SPF, DKIM, DMARC, MX and blocklist status. A domain with no check timestamp has never been checked, and the page says exactly that rather than showing a green tick by default.
- ▸ Answers are served from cache while fresh; a refresh re-queries DNS now.
- ▸ If the DNS engine is unreachable but a previous answer exists, that answer comes back flagged stale with the error attached. A six-hour-old DMARC record is useful and clearly labelled; an invented one is not.
- ▸ DKIM needs the selector to be checkable. Without one it is reported as unknown, not as passing.

chunks.page_title: Set up a sending pool and protect deliverab…
heading_path: Build a seed list you actually control
chunks.text: A seed address is a mailbox that receives placement probes. Add several across the providers your prospects use. The seed list is joined to your connected webmail accounts, which matters for the next step.

chunks.page_title: Set up a sending pool and protect deliverab…
chunks.text:
A placement test sends a probe to every seed and reports where it landed. Two behaviours are worth knowing before you read the result.

With no seed list, the test returns a "no seed list" status and an explanation. A placement test with nothing to send to has no result, and printing a made-up inbox percentage would be worse than printing nothing.

Placement itself is only claimed for seeds that are mailboxes your organization has connected — reading the destination folder is the only way to know where something landed. Every other seed is recorded as sent, with placement left null.

chunks.page_title: Set up a sending pool and protect deliverab…
chunks.text:
Health is scored over a rolling window from complaint rate, bounce rate and failure rate, with a bonus for engagement, and the page publishes the formula it used — the base score, the window, the minimum sample before a score means anything, each penalty, and the grade boundaries. It also publishes the auto-pause thresholds, so you know in advance what will pull a mailbox out of rotation and what it takes to bring it back.
- ▸ A mailbox below the minimum sample size does not get a confident grade. Small numbers are noise.
- ▸ When a mailbox is paused, the reason is recorded with it — including when the pause was automatic.

chunks.page_title: Take a deal from lead to signed contract to…
chunks.text: This walks the whole chain in the SalesShift web app. Each stage is its own section in the sidebar — Leads, Contacts, Deals, Products, Quotes, Contracts, Invoices, Subscriptions — and each one hands the next a document rather than a live reference. That is what stops a signed price from changing underneath you.

chunks.page_title: Take a deal from lead to signed contract to…
heading_path: Find the prospect and convert them
chunks.text:
Leads → Pool. Filter down, then open a person. Their address is masked until you spend a reveal on it. Revealing does not make them mailable — converting does, because conversion is what creates a contact and writes the consent metadata. Convert from the pool in one action and it will save, reveal if needed, and convert.
- ▸ Check the reveal meter first. The convert-from-pool result splits every id you passed into converted, already converted, skipped for no quota, skipped for no address, and skipped because the person was erased.
- ▸ Read all five buckets, including the zeros. A screen that shows only the successes is hiding a partial spend.

chunks.page_title: Take a deal from lead to signed contract to…
chunks.text: Deals shows your pipelines and their stages; a default pipeline is created on first use if you have none. Create a deal against the contact and set an amount and stage. Everything downstream — the quote, the contract, the invoice — can carry this deal id, which is what ties the paperwork back to the pipeline.

chunks.page_title: Take a deal from lead to signed contract to…
heading_path: Put the things you sell in the catalogue
chunks.text:
Products holds your catalogue: SKU, name, description, one-time or recurring, unit price in cents, currency, cost, tax rate, and — for recurring products — a billing interval and count, plus optional trial days. A recurring product without a billing interval is rejected, because a subscription with no period is not a thing.
- ▸ Prices are integer cents, not floats. That is deliberate — money that round-trips through a float eventually disagrees with itself.
- ▸ Deleting a product is a soft delete, so historic quotes and invoices keep their line references.

chunks.page_title: Take a deal from lead to signed contract to…
chunks.text:
Quotes → new. Attach the deal, the contact and the company, pick a currency and a validity date, then add lines. A line can reference a catalogue product or be free-text; either way it carries quantity, unit price, an optional line discount, and a tax rate. There is also an order-level discount.
- ▸ The line editor sends the whole grid and the server re-prices it. That is the contract on purpose: a failed call can never leave the document half-updated.
- ▸ A quote gets a generated document number when it is created.

chunks.page_title: Take a deal from lead to signed contract to…
chunks.text: Settings → Quotes holds the org-level numbering, tax and approval thresholds. Submitting a quote for approval either routes it to an approver or approves it outright when no rule is triggered. An approver can approve or decline the pending approval, and the decision is kept with the quote as history.

chunks.page_title: Take a deal from lead to signed contract to…
heading_path: Send it — this is where the contract appears
chunks.text: Sending a quote does three things in one action: it freezes the quote into a contract document, emails it to the recipient, and hands it to the e-signature flow. The recipient gets a link addressed by a token; there is also a public read-only view of the quote itself at its own token.

chunks.page_title: Take a deal from lead to signed contract to…
chunks.text:
The public signing page records the first open per party as a viewed event in the audit trail. A submitted signature is row-locked, so two simultaneous submissions cannot both sign. A party can also decline, with a reason.
- ▸ Contracts also accepts a document you already have — upload a PDF, DOCX, TXT, MD or HTML file and the content is extracted into an editable document that rides the same flow: edit, send, dual signatures, rendered PDF.
- ▸ Re-sending chases only the party who still owes a signature, rather than mailing everyone again.
- ▸ The executed PDF is rendered by the tenant node's Go e-sign engine: the document, the signature frames, a certificate of completion, and the audit trail. The sender gets their own copy of the same thing.

chunks.page_title: Take a deal from lead to signed contract to…
chunks.text: Invoices → create from the accepted quote, which carries its lines across. A brand-new invoice starts as a draft and can be edited freely: header fields, bill-to details, PO number, payment terms, currency, notes, and the line grid — which follows the same bulk-replace contract as the quote editor.

chunks.page_title: Take a deal from lead to signed contract to…
chunks.text: Issuing moves the invoice from draft to open. That stamps the issue date, derives the due date from the payment term, and freezes the bill-to snapshot. Freezing matters: if the customer changes their billing address next quarter, the invoice you already issued should not silently change with it.

chunks.page_title: Take a deal from lead to signed contract to…
chunks.text:
Sending emails the invoice with the PDF attached, from your own mailbox, with optional CC, subject and message. From there payment goes one of two ways.

Stripe: create a checkout session for the amount still outstanding. The customer pays, and the Stripe webhook — registered per payment integration — reconciles it back against the invoice.

Manually: record a bank transfer, cheque or cash payment against the invoice.

There is a public invoice page and a public PDF at a share token, so the customer never needs an account to see or pay it.
- ▸ The checkout session is for the amount still outstanding, so a part-payment recorded manually is reflected in what Stripe asks for.
- ▸ An invoice that was never paid can be voided. That is a cancellation, not a deletion — the record stays.

chunks.page_title: Take a deal from lead to signed contract to…
heading_path: If it recurs, put it on the ledger
chunks.text:
Subscriptions holds recurring revenue against a contact or company: create one, change the plan value, cancel immediately or at period end, reactivate a cancelled one. The MRR rollup is what the ledger exists for — it is the waterfall view of that revenue moving.

chunks.page_title: Self-Host vxcloud with the vxnode Container
heading_path: One container. Two ports. Five minutes.
chunks.text:
Copy these two commands. You will have a fully working vxnode listening on localhost when they finish.
```
docker pull vxcloud/vxnode:latest
```
```
docker run -d \
  --name vxcloud-vxnode \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  -p 8744:8744 \
  -p 8743:8743 \
  -v vxnode-data:/var/lib/vxnode \
  -e VXNODE_BIND=0.0.0.0 \
  -e VXNODE_DOMAIN=node1.vxcloud.io \
  vxcloud/vxnode:latest
```
vxnode now serves http://localhost:8744 . Continue below to expose it on the internet and register it with vxcloud.

```
curl -fsSL https://vxcloud.io/download/cli/install.sh | sh

# Verify, then sign in
```

chunks.page_title: Self-Host vxcloud with the vxnode Container
chunks.text:
vxnode talks HTTPS to the rest of the platform. If your machine sits behind NAT or a residential connection, the simplest path is a tunnel — pick whichever you already use. Both give you a managed TLS cert and a public hostname in under a minute, no router config.
```
# Install cloudflared, then expose vxnode over HTTPS via a free Cloudflare Tunnel.
cloudflared tunnel login
cloudflared tunnel create vxnode

# Map your hostname to the local vxnode port
cloudflared tunnel route dns vxnode node1.vxcloud.io
cloudflared tunnel run --url http://localhost:8744 vxnode

# Cloudflare now serves https://node1.vxcloud.io with a managed TLS cert.
```
Step 05

chunks.page_title: Self-Host vxcloud with the vxnode Container
chunks.text:
Last step: tell the vxcloud dashboard about your self-hosted node so workloads can be scheduled on it. You can do it from the CLI or from Nodes › Add node .
```
# Once vxnode is reachable over HTTPS, point vxcli at it and
# register it with your vxcloud workspace.
vxcli node add \
  --name primary \
  --endpoint https://node1.vxcloud.io \
  --port 8744 \
  --provider self-hosted

# Or use the dashboard: Nodes  ›  Add node  ›  Self-hosted (BYO)
```

vxnode runs anywhere Docker runs. vxcli on your laptop talks to it over HTTPS, and the vxcloud dashboard reads its public endpoint so your workloads schedule on your hardware.
- No outbound poll — vxnode is reached on its public hostname only.

- State persists in the /var/lib/vxnode volume — survives restarts and upgrades.

- 8743 TCP / HTTPS Admin / secondary (audit + ops)

heading_path: The six pillars of VxCloud security
chunks.text: Every feature on the platform is built against these six pillars. They map directly to SOC 2 trust service criteria, ISO 27001 Annex A, and the CIS Critical Security Controls.

heading_path: The six pillars of VxCloud security
chunks.text:
Every action on VxCloud is tied to an authenticated identity. Tenants federate their corporate IdP, enforce MFA on sensitive paths, and scope what each role can see and change down to a single resource.

heading_path: The six pillars of VxCloud security
chunks.text:
Data is encrypted at rest with AES-256 and in transit with TLS 1.3 — between your browser and VxCloud, between control-plane services, and between control plane and tenant nodes. Customer-managed encryption keys (CMK) are available on enterprise plans.
- AES-256-GCM at rest across managed databases, object storage, and Vault data
- TLS 1.3 with modern cipher suites; HSTS and forward secrecy on all public endpoints
- mTLS between control-plane services and tenant InstaNodeBox agents
- Customer-managed keys via AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP KMS, or self-hosted Vault Transit
- Encrypted backups stored across two geographic regions with versioned recovery

heading_path: The six pillars of VxCloud security
chunks.text:
Secrets, SSH key pairs, registry credentials, and API tokens never live in plaintext. VxCloud stores them in a per-tenant HashiCorp Vault namespace and resolves them just-in-time during deployments — your code stays clean of credentials.
- HashiCorp Vault per workspace with KVv2, AppRole, and JWT auth methods
- Dynamic secrets for databases, cloud providers, and Git providers
- SSH key pairs generated and stored server-side; private keys never leave Vault
- Docker registry credentials resolved at deploy time, scrubbed from container env
- Audit-trail of every secret read and write, retained 90+ days

heading_path: The six pillars of VxCloud security
chunks.text:
Tenant workloads run on isolated VPCs with security groups locked down by default. Inter-service traffic uses private routes; inbound exposure is opt-in per port. WAF and DDoS protection sit at the edge.
- Per-tenant VPCs and subnets across Alibaba, AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Linode, and bare metal
- Default-deny security groups; ports opened explicitly via the deployment wizard
- WAF rules for OWASP Top 10, bot mitigation, and rate limiting on edge endpoints
- DDoS protection via Cloudflare and provider-native scrubbing
- Optional VPN and VPC-peering for private connectivity between your network and VxCloud

heading_path: The six pillars of VxCloud security
chunks.text:
Every privileged action — provisioning, role changes, secret reads, deploys — is recorded in an append-only audit log. Stream the log to your SIEM, search it from the UI, and prove control activity to auditors.

- Real-time WebSocket stream and REST API for SIEM ingestion (Splunk, Datadog, ELK)

heading_path: Common challenges — and how VxCloud answers them
chunks.text:
Challenge
Engineering teams rotate fast; secrets sprawl across .env files, CI variables, and notebooks where nobody can find them — let alone revoke them.
How VxCloud solves it
A per-workspace HashiCorp Vault namespace stores every credential. Deployments resolve secrets just-in-time so code stays clean and revocation takes one click.
Challenge
Auditors ask for evidence that production access is least-privilege, MFA-enforced, and reviewed — and the screenshots take weeks to gather.
How VxCloud solves it
Append-only audit log captures every privileged action with actor, IP, and resource. Pre-built SOC 2 CC6 and ISO 27001 A.9 reports export in one click.
Challenge
Multi-region customers demand data residency guarantees, but your stack quietly replicates backups and logs across continents.
How VxCloud solves it
Pin tenant data, backups, and audit logs to one region. Control planes in US, EU, and Singapore; sub-processor list and SCCs published in the trust portal.
Challenge
A high-severity CVE drops on a Friday and nobody knows which images, clusters, or tenants are affected.
How VxCloud solves it
Continuous SBOM and CVE scanning per image, per cluster, per tenant. Weekly patch cadence with auto-generated tickets and one-click rolling restart.

Pick where your workloads run and where their data lives. VxCloud control planes are operated in the US, EU (Frankfurt), and Singapore. Tenant resources can be pinned to any region offered by AWS, Azure, GCP, or your own bare-metal nodes — your data never leaves the region you choose, including backups.
GDPR-compliant DPA, EU-based control plane, and Standard Contractual Clauses for any sub-processor transfers.
HIPAA BAA, CCPA disclosures, and FedRAMP-aligned controls for federal contractors.
Singapore PDPA, Australia Privacy Act, and India DPDP — data residency pinned to local regions.

heading_path: State on S3, GCS, Azure Blob, Postgres, Vault, or Consul
chunks.text:
Encrypted at rest with your CMK, locked by default, audited on every read and write. Click a backend to see the exact config and what you get for free.
```
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket         = "tf-state-prod"
    key            = "api/terraform.tfstate"
    region         = "us-east-1"
    encrypt        = true
    kms_key_id     = "alias/tf-state-cmk"
    dynamodb_table = "tf-state-locks"
    workspace_key_prefix = "ws"
  }
}
```
- Versioning + lifecycle for time-travel rollbacks
- KMS-CMK encryption at rest, TLS 1.3 in transit

heading_path: Dynamic credentials, resolved per apply, revoked on completion

- Postgres / MySQL / Mongo dynamic users with deterministic privileges
- PKI certificates auto-renewed before expiry — no cert outages
- KV v2 fallback for static secrets that must rotate on schedule

The CLI is the source of truth: vxcli cicd pipeline export --provider … emits the GitHub Actions YAML, GitLab CI YAML, or Jenkinsfile that runs the exact same stages. No copy-paste between syntaxes; no duplicated logic.
- Stages, parallelism, and strategy live in one declarative pipeline
- Provider-specific YAML stays generated — never hand-edited
- Pipeline diff in PRs shows the change, not the YAML noise
- Same vxcli runs in every CI image — predictable behaviour
```
# Same pipeline, four ways. Start with the CLI — it generates the
# provider-specific YAML for you on the way out.

# 1) Connect a Git provider (one-time)
vxcli cicd git connect github     # OAuth device flow, no copy-paste
vxcli cicd git connect gitlab
vxcli cicd git connect forgejo --url https://forge.acme.internal

# 2) Create a pipeline against any connected repo
vxcli cicd pipeline create \
  --name        studio-web        \
  --git-repo    prodxcloud/studio-web \
  --branch      main              \
  --on          push,pull_request \
  --stages      build,test,scan,deploy,verify \
  --deploy      kubernetes:prod-eu \
  --strategy    canary:25,sticky=10m,rollback=auto

# 3) Trigger / watch / debug
vxcli cicd pipeline trigger studio-web --branch main
vxcli cicd build list   --pipeline studio-web --status running
vxcli cicd build logs   <build-id>  --follow
vxcli cicd build show   <build-id>  --json | jq '.stages[].duration_ms'

# 4) Promote between environments with one command
vxcli cicd pipeline promote studio-web --from staging --to prod --canary 25
```

heading_path: A reasoning core, plus three specialists that do one job well
chunks.text: A universal /v1/ask dispatcher classifies each prompt and forwards it to the right backend. Every specialist gracefully falls back to its base model, so every route works from a clean checkout.

heading_path: Every answer is retrieved from your data, then reasoned over
chunks.text:
VxThinking encodes your CSVs, docs, and runbooks into a FAISS index with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 . The ReasoningEngine searches, analyzes, synthesizes, and decides — with two cache layers keeping repeat queries fast.
- L1 embeddings cache (TTL 1h) · L2 search cache (TTL 30m)
- GPU auto-detected; all four models share the device
- Provisioning intent returns a Golang payload for the agent
- Fully self-hosted — sovereign and air-gap friendly

chunks.text:
Hit /v1/ask and let the dispatcher route, or call a specialist directly. Train each model on your own datasets, build the FAISS index, and ship it as a single container on port 8745 .

```
# The universal dispatcher classifies your prompt and forwards it
# to the right specialist — no need to pick a model yourself.

curl -s http://llm.vxcloud.io/v1/ask \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"prompt":"Write a Terraform module for an S3 bucket with KMS"}' | jq .

# Force a specific model when you want fine control
curl -s http://llm.vxcloud.io/v1/ask \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"prompt":"Review this diff", "force_model":"codingllm"}' | jq .

# Inspect the keyword routing table
curl -s http://llm.vxcloud.io/v1/ask/routes | jq .
```

```
# Agent Control, scripted. Everything in the dashboard is a vxcli command.

# 1) Create an agent with a model, tools, and a knowledge base
vxcli agent create fieldops \
  --model      vxthinker:cloud \
  --tools      http,shell,provision \
  --knowledge  kb_fieldops \
  --prompt     prompts/fieldops-system.md

# 2) Attach a dataset and kick off a training run
vxcli dataset push ./data/fieldops.jsonl --name fieldops-sft
vxcli training start \
  --base   Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct \
  --dataset fieldops-sft \
  --method lora \
  --name   fieldops-rag-index

# 3) Watch the run live (loss, accuracy, GPU hours)
vxcli training list --status running
vxcli training logs <job-id> --follow

# 4) Deploy the fine-tuned model to an endpoint
vxcli model deploy fieldops-rag-index --endpoint fieldops-prod --gpu local-hf-offline
```

heading_path: The silent tax on every modern engineering team: lock-in
chunks.text:
Pick one cloud and you accept its pricing, its outages, its compliance footprint, and its acquisition risk. Pick three and you accept three teams' worth of glue code. There is no good answer at the platform level — only at the tooling level.
Multi-cloud is no longer aspirational. Regulated industries need Alibaba for China and AWS for the US. AI workloads need GPUs wherever they are cheapest this quarter. Acquired companies always come with the wrong cloud. The question is not whether your infrastructure will span clouds — it is whether you have the tooling to do it without doubling your SRE team.
The traditional answer is "use Terraform." Terraform is great at describing what you want; it is not great at the day-to-day imperative motions (provision a VM, SSH in, deploy an app, rotate a key) that fill most of an engineer's week. Cloud consoles solve the imperative side but lock you to one provider. vxcloud is the platform layer that gives you both — declarative IaC when you want it, an imperative CLI when you do not — and applies them uniformly across five clouds.
Every supported cloud sits behind the same HTTP surface. The CLI, the SDKs, and the Terraform provider all speak it. You learn the surface once.
EC2, GCE, Azure VM, ECS, and Linode Compute. One `provision` call, one returned object shape, the same SSH keypair flow on all five.
RDS, Aurora, Cloud SQL, Azure Database, ElastiCache, MemoryStore. Postgres, MySQL, Redis — one set of inputs (engine, size, region, network).
CIDR-block-first provisioning. Subnets, route tables, internet gateways, and security groups translated per-cloud automatically.
EKS, GKE, AKS. Define cluster name, node count, node type, region. The platform handles control-plane bootstrapping and kubeconfig delivery.
Lambda, Cloud Functions, Cloud Run, Azure Functions. Same code-zip + handler + runtime input, mapped to each provider's API.
S3, GCS, Azure Blob, OSS. IAM policy + role + keypair provisioning that lands in workspace Vault for downstream deploys.

heading_path: LLMs that can chat about your infrastructure are not the same as agents that can change it
chunks.text:
The gap between an AI assistant in your editor and an autonomous agent in production is enormous: credentials, audit trails, RBAC, rollback, cost caps, and multi-cloud translation. vxcloud is the platform that closes that gap.
The AI tooling market split early into two camps. The first — Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code, Continue — lives in your IDE and helps you write code. The second — n8n, Zapier AI, custom LangGraph deployments — lets you wire LLMs into business workflows, but assumes someone else built the infrastructure layer. Neither camp handles the actual work of operating a cloud.
The reason is unglamorous: cloud ops requires holding production credentials, recording every action, enforcing approval on destructive operations, capping spend per agent, and translating one intent ("deploy this") into five different cloud APIs. None of that is interesting research; all of it is required before a sane company will let an LLM near its AWS console. vxcloud is the platform layer that ships all of it as a default — so you can spend time on the agent prompts and the use cases, not on rebuilding RBAC for the fourth time.

heading_path: AgentControl: fine-tune agents that know your code
chunks.text:
The marketplace gets you a generic devops agent. AgentControl gets you a devops agent that has read your codebase, ticket history, and runbooks.
AgentControl is the training plane: a managed pipeline for fine-tuning small LLMs against your internal data and serving them as bound agents. The classic shape is: import a Git repo as a dataset, point at a Claude Haiku or Llama-3 base model, train, and the resulting agent is wired into a marketplace slot that anyone in the workspace can call.
```
import vxsdk
c = vxsdk.Client.load_from_vxcli()

# Import the repo as a JSONL dataset
ds = c.agentcontrol.github.import_dataset(
    repo="acme/platform", branch="main",
    include=["**/*.py", "docs/**/*.md"],
    exclude=["tests/**", "vendor/**"],
    dataset_name="acme-platform-snapshot",
)

# Fine-tune Claude Haiku on it
job = c.agentcontrol.fine_tuning.create(
    base_model="claude-haiku-4-5",
    dataset_id=ds["id"],
    name="acme-platform-coder-v1",
    hyperparameters={"epochs": 3, "learning_rate": 1e-5},
)

# Block until terminal status (succeeded / failed / cancelled)
job.wait_for_completion(timeout_seconds=3600)
print("model_id:", job.data.get("model_id"))

# The new agent is now in the marketplace under the trained model name
c.agentcontrol.agents.execute(
    agent_id="acme-platform-coder-v1",
    input="Refactor the metrics module to use OpenTelemetry SDK directly",
)
```

The platform features that turn an LLM toy into a tool a regulated company can deploy.
- Per-workspace HashiCorp Vault — agents never see plaintext cloud credentials.
- RBAC scoping — an agent gets exactly the toolset you grant it, no implicit root.
- Audit trail — every agent action recorded with input, output, and the human who delegated it.
- Approval gates — `resolveApproval()` pauses on destructive operations until a human signs off.
- Budget caps — per-agent daily and per-action spend ceilings prevent runaway loops.
- Bring Your Own Model — Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, Deepseek, Llama, Mistral, Ollama all supported via the chat envelope.
- Replay — re-run any past agent session deterministically for debugging or compliance review.
- Cross-cloud — agents work the same against AWS, GCP, Azure, Alibaba, and Linode — no per-cloud agent rewrites.

chunks.page_title: SSH Deploy Automation — Any VM You Own
heading_path: The Heroku workflow you can't have on Heroku anymore
chunks.text:
`git push heroku main` and an HTTPS URL — that was the easiest deploy story ever shipped. Then the free tier died, then the company entered sustaining mode. The workflow is what survived. vxcloud rebuilds it on top of any VM you already own.
The PaaS comfort — push code, get HTTPS, ignore servers — has migrated to Vercel, Render, Railway, and Fly over the past five years. Each of them is excellent inside its own walled garden. None of them runs on a VM you control. That means: you can't SSH in. You pay 5-10× the raw cloud cost at scale. You can't run the runtime you actually want. And if the platform ever raises prices or sunsets a region, you re-deploy from scratch on something else.
vxcloud's answer is unglamorous: keep the PaaS-style CLI workflow, but target a regular Linux VM over SSH. The VM can be on AWS, GCP, Azure, Alibaba, Linode, a bare-metal box at Hetzner, or your home lab. The deploy command is the same. The SSL automation is the same. The rollback is the same. You pay your own cloud bill and you keep root.

- [Take a deal from lead to signed contract to paid invoice](https://vxcloud.io/docs/guides/salesshift-lead-to-contract-to-invoice): The full quote-to-cash path: reveal and convert a prospect, open a deal, price it from the product catalogue, send a quote that freezes into an e-signable contract, then invoice it and take payment through Stripe or record it manually.

vxcli node add — Register a self-hosted vxnode container (BYO hardware: Docker / bare-metal / Tailscale Funnel / Cloudflare Tunnel). Mirrors the dashboard's "Self-Hosted" form — POSTs to /api/v1/auth/nodes/self-hosted. Bare hostname or full https:// URL both accepted.
Usage: vxcli node add --endpoint <url> [--hostname N] [--port 8744] [--tunnel cloudflare|tailscale|caddy|direct] [--key-pair-name K] [--description "…"] [--set-default] [--skip-verify]
Flags:
- --endpoint: Public HTTPS URL of the vxnode container (required). Bare hostname accepted — https:// is prepended.
- --hostname: Friendly label (default: derived from --endpoint host)
- --port: API port the Go/Gin server listens on (default 8744)
- --public-ip: Optional static public IP (skip when using a tunnel)
- --private-ip: Optional LAN IP (diagnostics only)
- --tunnel: How TLS terminates: cloudflare | tailscale | caddy | direct (default cloudflare)
- --key-pair-name: Vault key-pair name to attach for SSH-based provisioning
- --ide-token: IDE connection token from `docker logs vxcloud-vxnode`
- --agent1-token: Optional Agent-1 connection token
- --storage: Storage type: ssd | hdd | nvme (documentation only)
- --backup: Backup mode: none | daily | weekly (documentation only)
- --description: Free-text note shown in the nodes list
- --ssh-user: SSH username on the host (only stored if set)
- --set-default: Mark the new node as your default target after registering
- --skip-verify: Skip the post-register handshake against the node's /health endpoint
Example:

```bash
# Marketing-site minimal form
vxcli node add --endpoint https://node1.vxcloud.io
# ✓ node "node1.vxcloud.io" registered with workspace (id=49)

# Full self-hosted with Cloudflare Tunnel + vault key + default switch
vxcli node add \
  --endpoint https://prod-east-1.example.com \
  --hostname prod-east-1 --port 8744 \
  --tunnel cloudflare \
```

Provision an application onto a remote VM. The CLI bundles your source (or clones a repo), POSTs it to the tenant node, and the node SSHs into the target VM to build, run, and front the app with nginx (or Traefik in SSL mode). All subcommands share the SSH flag set and the SSL flag set. HTTPS modes — `deploy container --enable-ssl` installs host systemd nginx + certbot in front of the first --port; `deploy <stack> --enable-ssl` (fastapi/react/nextjs/django/golang/...) bootstraps the shared `vxcloud-traefik` container which fronts the docker-compose stack on :443 with a Let's Encrypt cert. Both require the domain's A record to already point at --host. Stack deploys also require the keypair to be uploaded to Vault first (`vxcli configure setup vm --pem-file ./mykey.pem --key-pair-name MYKEY`).

vxcli deploy container — Deploy a single Docker container by image. The image is pulled and run on the remote VM with the supplied port mappings, env vars, and restart policy.
Usage: vxcli deploy container <name> --image <image> --host <h> --ssh-user <u> --key-pair-name <k> --port <host:container> [--env KEY=val] [--restart unless-stopped]
Flags:
- --image: Image reference (e.g. grafana/grafana:latest, registry/team/api:1.4)
- --port: Port mapping host:container (repeatable)
- --env: Environment variable KEY=value (repeatable)
- --volume: Volume mapping /host:/container (repeatable)
- --restart: Restart policy: always | unless-stopped | on-failure | no (default unless-stopped)
- --network: Docker network to attach the container to
- --docker-user: Registry username for private images
- --docker-pass: Registry password/token for private images
- --container-name: Container name on the host (defaults to <name>)
- --cap-add: Linux capability to add (repeatable)
- --device: Host device to map (repeatable, e.g. /dev/net/tun)
- --sysctl: Sysctl key=value (repeatable)
- --command: Override container command. NOTE: the value is comma-split server-side and quotes are stripped — only safe for comma-free single tokens like `--config=/etc/app/config.yaml` or `server -dev`. For structured config (JSON/YAML), write it to a host file and use `--volume`.
- --enable-ssl: Front the deployed service with HTTPS + a Let's Encrypt cert. For `deploy container` this installs host nginx + certbot in front of the first --port; for stack deploys (fastapi/react/nextjs/django/golang/etc.) this routes through the shared Traefik container on :443.
- --domain: Public domain for the HTTPS endpoint (required with --enable-ssl). The A record must already resolve to --host before the deploy runs — Let's Encrypt validates via HTTP-01 on port 80.
- --ssl-email: Let's Encrypt contact email used during ACME registration / for expiry notices. Defaults to info@prodxcloud.com.
- --expose-direct-port: (stack deploys) In SSL mode, ALSO publish the raw nginx/host port alongside the Traefik :443 route — so both `https://domain` and `http://ip:port` reach the app.
- --host: Target VM hostname or IP (required)
- --ssh-user: SSH username on the target VM (required)
- --key-pair-name: Vault key-pair name (required, unless --key-pair-location is set). Upload first via `vxcli configure setup vm --key-pair-name <N> --pem-file <p.pem>`.
- --key-pair-location: Path to a local PEM file (e.g. ./mykey.pem or ~/.ssh/id_rsa); alternative to --key-pair-name. NOTE: `deploy fastapi/react/nextjs/...` (stack deploys) IGNORE this — the server-side request is form-validated against a Vault `key_pair_name` only. Use `vxcli configure setup vm` first. `deploy container` accepts both.
- --organization: Organization name for workspace isolation (defaults to --workspace-user, then to authenticated username)
- --workspace-user: Override workspace owner used for vault lookup (defaults to authenticated username). Use when AWSPRODKEY2 etc. lives in another user’s workspace.
Basic (public image):
```bash
vxcli deploy container grafana \
  --image grafana/grafana:latest \
  --host 13.216.243.13 --ssh-user ubuntu \
  --key-pair-name AWSPRODKEY1.PEM \
  --port 3000:3000 --restart unless-stopped
```

```bash

# Requires: grafana.example.com A record -> 13.216.243.13 already set.
vxcli deploy container grafana \
  --image grafana/grafana:latest \
  --host 13.216.243.13 --ssh-user ubuntu \
  --key-pair-name AWSPRODKEY1.PEM \
  --port 3000:3000 --restart unless-stopped \
  --enable-ssl --domain grafana.example.com --ssl-email ops@example.com
```

vxcli deploy static — Deploy a static-site bundle (HTML/CSS/JS, no build step) — uploaded over SSH and served by **host systemd nginx** (NOT the Docker/Traefik path). This means the VM CANNOT already be running another `deploy <stack>` (Traefik would already own host port 80/443). For SSL pair this with `vxcli install certbot --arg --domain=<d> --arg --email=<e>` which uses the certbot nginx plugin to add a 443 server block in place.
Usage: vxcli deploy static <path|--repo-url> --host <h> --ssh-user <u> --key-pair-name <k> [--domain D]
Flags:
- <path>: Local source directory (default '.')
- --repo-url: Git repository URL — clones on the VM instead of uploading
- --branch: Git branch (default: main)
- --app-name: Application name (used as nginx site name)
- --http-port: HTTP port nginx serves on (default 80)
- --domain: Sets server_name in the generated nginx config. Required if you intend to obtain a cert with certbot afterward.
Example:
```bash
# 1. Deploy the static bundle (host nginx on :80)
vxcli deploy static --repo-url https://github.com/me/landing \
  --host 52.71.204.251 --ssh-user ubuntu --key-pair-name MYKEY \
  --app-name landing --http-port 80 --domain landing.example.com

# 2. Add HTTPS via certbot
vxcli install certbot \
  --host 52.71.204.251 --ssh-user ubuntu --key-pair-name MYKEY \
  --arg --domain --arg landing.example.com \
  --arg --email --arg ops@example.com
```

--pg-db --host --ssh-user --key-pair-name Flags: - --resource-name: Logical name for the DB (used as Vault path + dashboard label) - --pg-user: Postgres superuser to create - --pg-password: Password for the superuser (also written to Vault) - --pg-db: Initial database to create - --pg-version: PostgreSQL major version (default 16) - --pg-port: TCP port to expose (default 5432) Example: ```bash vxcli deploy metaldb \ --resource-name prod-pg \ --pg-user app --pg-password "$PG_PASSWORD" --pg-db app \ --host 13.216.243.13 --ssh-user ubuntu --key-pair-name AWSPRODKEY1.PEM ```

vxcli deploy metaldb \
  --resource-name prod-pg \
  --pg-user app --pg-password "$PG_PASSWORD" --pg-db app \
  --host 13.216.243.13 --ssh-user ubuntu --key-pair-name AWSPRODKEY1.PEM

vxcli install <tech> — Install one of the catalog services on the remote VM. Each entry supports baremetal, docker, or kubernetes mode; pick with --mode.
Usage: vxcli install <tech> --mode <baremetal|docker|kubernetes> --host <h> --ssh-user <u> --key-pair-name <k>
Flags:
- <tech>: Service from the catalog (e.g. postgres, grafana, ollama, openclaw, kafka, mongodb, nginx, redis)
- --mode: Install mode: baremetal | docker | kubernetes (default baremetal)
- --arg: Extra positional arg appended to the install script (repeatable)
- --host: Target VM hostname or IP (required)
- --ssh-user: SSH username on the target VM (required)
- --key-pair-name: Vault key-pair name (required, unless --key-pair-location is set). Upload first via `vxcli configure setup vm --key-pair-name <N> --pem-file <p.pem>`.
- --key-pair-location: Path to a local PEM file (e.g. ./mykey.pem or ~/.ssh/id_rsa); alternative to --key-pair-name. NOTE: `deploy fastapi/react/nextjs/...` (stack deploys) IGNORE this — the server-side request is form-validated against a Vault `key_pair_name` only. Use `vxcli configure setup vm` first. `deploy container` accepts both.
- --organization: Organization name for workspace isolation (defaults to --workspace-user, then to authenticated username)
- --workspace-user: Override workspace owner used for vault lookup (defaults to authenticated username). Use when AWSPRODKEY2 etc. lives in another user’s workspace.
Docker mode:
```bash
# Most catalog services support docker mode out of the box.
vxcli install grafana --mode docker \
  --host 44.220.145.108 --ssh-user ubuntu \
  --key-pair-name AWSPRODKEY1.PEM
```
Baremetal mode:
```bash
# Run the underlying systemd service directly on the host.
vxcli install postgres --mode baremetal \
  --host 44.220.145.108 --ssh-user ubuntu \
  --key-pair-name AWSPRODKEY1.PEM \
  --arg --version=16
```
Kubernetes mode:
```bash
# Install via the bundled Helm chart against the active kubeconfig.
vxcli install kafka --mode kubernetes \
  --host 44.220.145.108 --ssh-user ubuntu \
  --key-pair-name AWSPRODKEY1.PEM
```
AI: Ollama + OpenClaw:
```bash
vxcli install ollama --mode docker \
  --host 44.220.145.108 --ssh-user ubuntu \
  --key-pair-name AWSPRODKEY1.PEM

vxcli install openclaw --mode docker \
  --host 44.220.145.108 --ssh-user ubuntu \
  --key-pair-name AWSPRODKEY1.PEM
```
