vxcli sessions list — List recent provisioning sessions for the active node, with status and duration. Equivalent to the Monitoring tab in the dashboard.
Usage: vxcli sessions list [--limit N] [--status <state>] [--json]
Flags:
- --limit: Number of sessions to return (default 20)
- --status: Filter by state: running | completed | failed
- --json: Emit JSON for piping into jq / scripts
Recent:
```bash
vxcli sessions list --limit 10
```
Failed only:
```bash
vxcli sessions list --status failed
```
JSON for jq:
```bash
vxcli sessions list --status failed --json \
  | jq '.[] | {id, app, started_at, error}'
```

vxcli marketplace agent deploy — Deploy a marketplace agent onto a target VM. The server stages the agent's source (`shared/development/agents/<id>`) into a session, layers a `.env` from `--system-prompt` + `--env-vars`, and ships the Docker bundle via the standard SSH-deploy script. **NOTE:** the current node-side handler does NOT emit `enable_ssl`/`domain` tfvars — for HTTPS deploy the same agent source via `vxcli deploy fastapi/golang --enable-ssl --domain` instead.
Usage: vxcli marketplace agent deploy <agent_id> --host <h> --ssh-user <u> --key-pair-name <k> [--system-prompt "…"] [--env-vars "KEY=v\nKEY2=v2"]
Flags:
- --agent-name: Display name (defaults to <agent_id>)
- --app-port: Container port (defaults to the agent's catalog default — 8000 for most, 8002 for chromadb)
- --http-port: Host nginx port (default 80)
- --system-prompt: System prompt baked into the agent's .env (LLM agents)
- --env-vars: Newline-separated KEY=value env vars (e.g. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=…)
- --version: Agent version tag (default 1.0.0)
- --host: Target VM hostname or IP (required)
- --ssh-user: SSH username on the target VM (required)
- --key-pair-name: Vault key-pair name (required, unless --key-pair-location is set). Upload first via `vxcli configure setup vm --key-pair-name <N> --pem-file <p.pem>`.
- --key-pair-location: Path to a local PEM file (e.g. ./mykey.pem or ~/.ssh/id_rsa); alternative to --key-pair-name. NOTE: `deploy fastapi/react/nextjs/...` (stack deploys) IGNORE this — the server-side request is form-validated against a Vault `key_pair_name` only. Use `vxcli configure setup vm` first. `deploy container` accepts both.
- --organization: Organization name for workspace isolation (defaults to --workspace-user, then to authenticated username)
- --workspace-user: Override workspace owner used for vault lookup (defaults to authenticated username). Use when AWSPRODKEY2 etc. lives in another user’s workspace.
Example:
```bash
vxcli marketplace agent deploy prompt_agent \
  --host 13.216.243.13 --ssh-user ubuntu --key-pair-name AWSPRODKEY1.PEM \
  --system-prompt "You are a senior SRE on call." \
  --env-vars $'ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-…\nMODEL=claude-sonnet-4-6'
```

heading_path: Vault keypair upload is a prerequisite for stack deploys
chunks.text:
Vault keypair upload is a prerequisite for stack deploys — `vxcli deploy fastapi/react/nextjs/django/golang/...` resolves SSH keys ONLY from the workspace Vault (the form-validator rejects requests without `key_pair_name`, and the handler ignores `private_key_pem`). `--key-pair-location` is honored by `deploy container` but silently dropped by stack deploys. Always upload first.
Usage: vxcli configure setup vm --key-pair-name <N> --pem-file <p.pem>
Example:
```bash
vxcli configure setup vm \
  --key-pair-name AWSPRODKEY1 \
  --pem-file ~/.ssh/aws-prod.pem
```

`deploy container --command` is comma-split server-side — Whatever you pass to `--command` is forwarded to the node, which splits on every `,` and strips quotes before handing it to `docker run`. Inline structured config (JSON / multi-key YAML) WILL be destroyed. Only safe for comma-free single tokens.
Usage: # BAD (mangled): --command '--config=yaml:{"receivers":{...}}' 
# GOOD: stage a config file on the host and reference it.
Example:
```bash
# 1. Stage the config (one-time):
scp otelcol-config.yaml ubuntu@host:/opt/otelcol-config.yaml

# 2. Deploy:
vxcli deploy container opentelemetry \
  --image otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:latest \
  --volume /opt/otelcol-config.yaml:/etc/otelcol-contrib/config.yaml \
  --command '--config=/etc/otelcol-contrib/config.yaml' \
  --port 13133:13133 --port 4318:4318 \
  --enable-ssl --domain otel.example.com --ssl-email ops@example.com \
  --host h --ssh-user u --key-pair-name k
```

heading_path: TCP services 502 on the HTTPS endpoint (postgres, redis, …)
chunks.text:
TCP services 502 on the HTTPS endpoint (postgres, redis, …) — `--enable-ssl` puts an HTTP nginx proxy in front of `--port`. Nginx HTTP cannot speak postgres/redis/etc. wire protocols, so `https://<domain>` returns 502. The deploy itself is fine (cert issued, container up); the DB is reachable on its raw port. For genuine TLS on the DB you need to mount the LE cert into the container and configure native TLS there.
Usage: # Connect direct, not via the HTTPS endpoint
Example:
```bash
# After: vxcli deploy container postgres --port 5432:5432 --enable-ssl --domain db.example.com …
psql -h db.example.com -p 5432 -U vxadmin -d vxcloud   # works
curl https://db.example.com/                            # 502 — expected
```

heading_path: React/Next nginx healthcheck races IPv6 — container reports unhealthy → Traefik 404s
chunks.text:
React/Next nginx healthcheck races IPv6 — container reports unhealthy → Traefik 404s — The Docker template healthcheck is `wget --spider http://localhost/health`. Inside the container `localhost` resolves to `::1` first, but the nginx sidecar binds IPv4-only (`listen 80;`) → "connection refused" → container goes `unhealthy` → Traefik drops it → public domain returns 404 + the TRAEFIK DEFAULT CERT. Fix: add an IPv6 listener and reload.
Usage: docker exec <container> sh -c 'sed -i "/listen 80;/a    listen [::]:80;" $CONF && nginx -s reload'
Example:
```bash
# For deploy react / deploy nextjs sidecars
docker exec app-myapp sh -c \
  'sed -i "/listen 80;/a    listen [::]:80;" /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf && nginx -s reload'
```

heading_path: Co-hosting two stack deploys on one VM collides via docker-compose v1
chunks.text:
Co-hosting two stack deploys on one VM collides via docker-compose v1 — Every stack deploy lands at `/opt/<type>-deploy/bin/docker-compose-<uuid>.yml`. docker-compose v1 keys containers by `(project, service)` and the project name comes from the parent dir basename — `bin` for every deploy. If both deploys define a service literally named `nginx`, the second `up --force-recreate` tries to recreate the FIRST deploy's nginx (by project+service), failing if the image is gone. Workaround when troubleshooting: re-run with a unique project name (`-p <unique>`).
Usage: docker-compose -p <unique-name> -f bin/docker-compose-<uuid>.yml up -d --build
Example:
```bash
# Recover from a collided redeploy without disturbing the other app:
cd /opt/nextjs-deploy
docker-compose -p nextjsapp -f bin/docker-compose-<uuid>.yml up -d --build
```

heading_path: sebp/elk is too heavy for small VMs — use single-node Elasticsearch
chunks.text:
sebp/elk is too heavy for small VMs — use single-node Elasticsearch — `sebp/elk` runs Elasticsearch + Logstash + Kibana in one container = 3 JVMs. Even on 11 GB RAM the startup spike drives load avg over 30 and pegs SSH. Prefer the official single-node Elasticsearch image for `vxcli deploy container` ELK demos.
Usage: vxcli deploy container elasticsearch --image docker.elastic.co/elasticsearch/elasticsearch:8.15.3 …
Example:
```bash
# vm.max_map_count must be 262144+ on the host first.
sudo sysctl -w vm.max_map_count=262144

vxcli deploy container elasticsearch \
  --image docker.elastic.co/elasticsearch/elasticsearch:8.15.3 \
  --env discovery.type=single-node \
  --env xpack.security.enabled=false \
  --env xpack.security.enrollment.enabled=false \
  --env ES_JAVA_OPTS=-Xmx1g \
  --port 9200:9200 \
  --host h --ssh-user u --key-pair-name k \
  --enable-ssl --domain es.example.com --ssl-email ops@example.com

heading_path: Cloudflare HTTP 524 on long deploys ≠ failure
chunks.text:
Cloudflare HTTP 524 on long deploys ≠ failure — node1.vxcloud.io is fronted by Cloudflare with a ~120s proxy-read timeout. Deploys that need a big image pull / multi-minute build will surface as `HTTP 524` to the CLI, but the deploy keeps running on the node. Don't retry blindly — that starts a duplicate job. Instead poll the VM (`docker ps`) or `vxcli sessions list` for the new session.
Usage: # After a 524, poll the VM rather than re-running
Example:
```bash
ssh <user>@<host> 'sudo docker ps -a --format "{{.Names}}:{{.Status}}"'
vxcli sessions list --status running
```

import vxsdk
# Or equivalently: `import vxcloud` (alias package — same code).

    domain="grafana.example.com",
    ssl_email="[email protected]",

)

Client construction & authentication — Two constructors — explicit credentials or load from `~/.vxcloud/credentials.json` (the file `vxcli auth login` writes). Auto-refresh JWT on 401.
Explicit credentials:
```
import vxsdk

c = vxsdk.Client(
    api_key="xc_live_…",
    username="your-username",
    # optional overrides:
    # vxcloud_url="https://api.vxcloud.io",
    # node_url="https://node1.vxcloud.io",
)
print(c.whoami)
```
Load from vxcli:
```
import vxsdk

c = vxsdk.Client.load_from_vxcli()
c.authenticate()    # eager JWT exchange (optional — refreshes lazily)
print(c.whoami.username)
```
Async flavor:
```
import asyncio
from vxsdk_async import AsyncClient
# Equivalent: `from vxsdk_async import VxCloud` or `vxcloud` — same class.

async def main():
    async with AsyncClient.load_from_vxcli() as c:
        for n in await c.nodes.list():
            print(n["name"], n.get("url"))

asyncio.run(main())
```
Brand-name aliases (vxsdk / vxcloud / VxCloud):
```
# All four import / class combinations below resolve to the SAME class —
# pick the name your team prefers. There is no behavior difference.

# 1. Canonical: `vxsdk.Client`
import vxsdk
c = vxsdk.Client.load_from_vxcli()

# 2. PascalCase brand alias (mirrors the TypeScript SDK)
c = vxsdk.VxCloud.load_from_vxcli()

# 3. Lowercase brand alias
c = vxsdk.vxcloud.load_from_vxcli()

# 4. Alias package — `pip install vxcloud` (depends on vxsdk)
import vxcloud
c = vxcloud.Client.load_from_vxcli()
c = vxcloud.load_from_vxcli()      # module-level convenience helper

print(c.whoami.username)
```

deploy (container + 14 stacks) — Deploy any Docker image, or any of the 14 supported stacks (fastapi, react, nextjs, django, nodejs, python, golang, rust, cpp, php, static, angular, vuejs, expo, flask, java, laravel, metaldb). Single-command HTTPS via `enable_ssl` + `domain` (host-nginx+certbot for `container`; shared Traefik for stack deploys).
Docker container (HTTPS, single call):
```
# Installs host nginx + Let's Encrypt cert in front of the first port (3000).
# Requires: grafana.example.com A record -> 13.216.243.13 already set.
result = c.deploy.container(
    image="grafana/grafana:latest",
    name="grafana",
    ports=["3000:3000"],
    env=["GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD=changeme"],
    restart="unless-stopped",
    enable_ssl=True,
    domain="grafana.example.com",
    ssl_email="ops@example.com",
    host="13.216.243.13", ssh_user="ubuntu",
    key_pair_name="AWSPRODKEY1",
)
print(result["session_id"], result.get("ssl_certificate_status"))
```
Vault (dev mode, HTTPS):
```
# IPC_LOCK avoids swapping secrets to disk; `server -dev` runs
# the in-memory dev server with the supplied root token.
result = c.deploy.container(
    image="hashicorp/vault:latest",
    name="vault",
    command="server -dev",
    cap_add=["IPC_LOCK"],            # patched into the SDK; safe to pass
    env=[
        "VAULT_DEV_ROOT_TOKEN_ID=devroot",
        "VAULT_DEV_LISTEN_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0:8200",
    ],
    ports=["8200:8200"],
    enable_ssl=True,
    domain="vault.example.com",
    ssl_email="ops@example.com",
    host="13.216.243.13", ssh_user="ubuntu",
    key_pair_name="AWSPRODKEY1",
)
```
OpenTelemetry w/ mounted config:
```
# Stage the config on the VM first (one-time):

    image="otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:latest",
    name="opentelemetry",

    command="--config=/etc/otelcol-contrib/config.yaml",  # NO commas!
    ports=["13133:13133", "4318:4318", "4317:4317"],
    enable_ssl=True,
    domain="otel.example.com",
    ssl_email="ops@example.com",
    host="13.216.243.13", ssh_user="ubuntu",
    key_pair_name="AWSPRODKEY1",
)
```
PostgreSQL (DB on :5432; HTTPS is informational):
```
# Postgres is a TCP service — the HTTPS endpoint nginx fronts will 502
# (HTTP nginx can't speak postgres wire protocol). Connect via psql on
# port 5432; the cert/domain exist for DNS + future native-TLS work.

    image="postgres:16",
    name="postgres",
    env=["POSTGRES_PASSWORD=changeme", "POSTGRES_DB=app", "POSTGRES_USER=app"],
    ports=["5432:5432"],
    enable_ssl=True,
    domain="db.example.com",
    ssl_email="ops@example.com",
    host="13.216.243.13", ssh_user="ubuntu",
    key_pair_name="AWSPRODKEY1",
)

services (lifecycle + host ops) — Start / stop / restart / remove / status of a Docker container, plus host-level reboot, cleanup, and diagnostics under `services.vm`.
Container lifecycle:
```
ssh = dict(host="203.0.113.24", ssh_user="ubuntu",
           key_pair_name="AWSPRODKEY1.PEM")

# List
for line in c.services.list(**ssh).get("output", "").splitlines():
    print(line)

# Status of one container
print(c.services.status("studio-backend", **ssh))

# Lifecycle
c.services.start("studio-backend", **ssh)
c.services.stop("studio-backend", **ssh)
c.services.restart("studio-backend", **ssh)
c.services.remove("studio-backend", **ssh)
# Logs (systemd unit only)
c.services.logs("ollama", tail=200, **ssh)
```
Host-level operations (services.vm.*):
```
# Cleanup
c.services.vm.disk_cleanup(**ssh)
c.services.vm.docker_cleanup(**ssh)
c.services.vm.restart_docker(**ssh)

# Diagnostics
print(c.services.vm.memory(**ssh).get("output"))
print(c.services.vm.disk(**ssh).get("output"))
print(c.services.vm.list_services(**ssh).get("output"))

# Targeted ops
c.services.vm.kill_port(8000, **ssh)
c.services.vm.stop_service("postgresql", **ssh)

# Destructive — confirm upstream before calling
# c.services.vm.reboot(**ssh)
# c.services.vm.shutdown(**ssh)
```

cloud (vm / s3 / iam / network / database / kubernetes / serverless) — Per-provider helpers covering VM lifecycle, storage, IAM, networking, managed databases, Kubernetes, and serverless functions. The `c.cloud.vm.*` namespace mirrors the TypeScript SDK; the flat `c.cloud.create_*(...)` methods are kept for back-compat.
VM — provision / status / action (symmetric API):
```
# Preferred: `c.cloud.vm.*` mirrors the TypeScript SDK.
vm = c.cloud.vm.provision(
    name="api-vm", cloud="aws", region="us-east-1",
    instance_type="t3.small", key_pair_name="AWSPRODKEY2",
    tags={"env": "staging"},
)
print(vm["public_ip"])

# Lifecycle control
state = c.cloud.vm.status(instance_id=vm["instance_id"], cloud="aws")
c.cloud.vm.action(instance_id=vm["instance_id"], action="restart", cloud="aws")
# action must be one of: start | stop | restart | reboot

# Legacy flat alias still works:
# vm = c.cloud.create_vm(name="api-vm", ...)
```
S3 / IAM / keypair:
```

c.cloud.create_iam_policy("read-only-s3", policy_document={
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [{"Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:Get*", "Resource": "*"}],
})

c.cloud.create_iam_role("svc-api-role", assume_role_policy={
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [{
        "Effect": "Allow",
        "Principal": {"Service": "ec2.amazonaws.com"},
        "Action": "sts:AssumeRole",
    }],
})

agentcontrol (full /api/v2/agentcontrol/* surface — 22 sub-resources) — Full UI parity with the AgentControl dashboard at /dashboard/?tab=agentcontrol. Original surfaces (fine_tuning, training, knowledge, datasets, ac_agents, github) plus the new sub-resources: embeddings, tools, mcp, evals, code, models, deployments, web_assets, benchmarks, catalog, health, events, llm, deploy_targets, workflows, infra. Plus `runtime_metrics(endpoint)` to proxy a marketplace agent's /metrics scrape through the node. Every call sends `X-Tenant-ID` automatically; pass `tenant_id=` per call to override.
summary + list resources:
```
# Top-level dashboard summary — counts, recent activity, etc.

print(summary.get("total_models"), summary.get("active_training_jobs"))

# Browse each surface

    print("FT:", j["id"], j.get("status"))

for t in c.agentcontrol.training.list():
    print("Train:", t["id"], t.get("status"))

for k in c.agentcontrol.knowledge.list():
    print("KB:", k["id"], k.get("name"))

for d in c.agentcontrol.datasets.list():
    print("DS:", d["id"], d.get("row_count"))
```
Fine-tune a base model and wait for completion:
```
# Start a fine-tuning job
job = c.agentcontrol.fine_tuning.create(
    base_model="claude-haiku-4-5",
    dataset_id="ds-abc123",
    name="support-tone-v1",
    hyperparameters={"epochs": 3, "learning_rate": 1e-5},
)

# Poll until terminal (succeeded / failed / cancelled)
# `wait_for_completion` blocks; pass `timeout_seconds` to bound it.
job.wait_for_completion(timeout_seconds=3600, interval_seconds=10)
print("Final status:", job.status, "· model_id:", job.data.get("model_id"))

# Same shape works for training & knowledge:
#   c.agentcontrol.training.create(...).wait_for_completion()
#   c.agentcontrol.knowledge.create(...).wait_for_completion()

metaldb (self-managed PostgreSQL over SSH) — Provision and verify a self-managed PostgreSQL instance on a customer VM. The platform installs Postgres, opens the firewall, creates the user/database, and stores the resulting connection string in workspace Vault under `metaldb/<resource>`. Use this when you want full DB lifecycle ownership instead of a managed RDS / Aurora.
provision + test_connection:
```
# Provision Postgres on an existing VM via SSH. Credentials are minted
# by the platform and written to Vault — no plaintext password leaves the
# call. Returns the connection string + Vault path.
result = c.metaldb.provision(
    resource_name="app-metaldb",
    host="203.0.113.24", ssh_user="ubuntu",
    key_pair_name="AWSPRODKEY1",       # MUST be in Vault
    db_name="app", db_user="app",
    pg_version="16",
    port=5432,
    listen_address="0.0.0.0",
)
print(result["connection_string"], "·", result.get("vault_path"))

# Verify connectivity from the same node (does not require client psql)
ok = c.metaldb.test_connection(
    host="203.0.113.24",
    port=5432, db_name="app", db_user="app",
    vault_path=result["vault_path"],   # password is fetched from Vault
)
print("reachable:", ok.get("connected"))
```

Production notes & known issues — Real failure modes you will hit at least once. Same content as the CLI "Operational gotchas" section, adapted to SDK usage.
Keypair MUST be in Vault for stack deploys:
```
# c.deploy.stack("fastapi"/"react"/"nextjs"/...) resolves SSH keys ONLY
# from the workspace Vault. The server's form-validator rejects requests
# without `key_pair_name`, and `private_key_pem` is ignored. Upload first:
#
#   vxcli configure setup vm --key-pair-name MYKEY --pem-file ./mykey.pem
#
# c.deploy.container DOES accept private_key_pem as a fallback.
```
`command=` is comma-split server-side:
```
# The container deploy endpoint comma-splits `command` and strips quotes
# before handing it to `docker run`. Inline structured config WILL be
# destroyed. Only safe for comma-free single tokens.
#
# BAD (mangled):
#   c.deploy.container(command='--config=yaml:{"receivers":{...}}', ...)
#
# GOOD: stage a config file on the host, then use --volume:
c.deploy.container(
    image="otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:latest",
    volumes=["/opt/otelcol-config.yaml:/etc/otelcol-contrib/config.yaml"],
    command="--config=/etc/otelcol-contrib/config.yaml",  # no commas
    ports=["13133:13133", "4318:4318"],
    enable_ssl=True, domain="otel.example.com", ssl_email="ops@example.com",
    host="h", ssh_user="u", key_pair_name="k",
)
```
TCP services 502 on the HTTPS endpoint:
```
# --enable-ssl puts an HTTP nginx proxy in front of --port. Nginx HTTP
# cannot speak postgres/redis/etc. wire protocols, so https://<domain>
# returns 502. The deploy itself is fine — DB is reachable on its raw port.
c.deploy.container(
    image="postgres:16", name="postgres",
    env=["POSTGRES_PASSWORD=changeme"],
    ports=["5432:5432"],
    enable_ssl=True, domain="db.example.com", ssl_email="ops@example.com",
    host="h", ssh_user="u", key_pair_name="k",
)
# psql -h db.example.com -p 5432 -U postgres   # works
# curl https://db.example.com/                 # 502 — expected
```
Cloudflare HTTP 524 on slow deploys ≠ failure:
```
# node1.vxcloud.io is fronted by Cloudflare with a ~120s proxy-read
# timeout. Big image pulls / multi-minute builds surface as a 524, but
# the deploy keeps running. Don't retry blindly — poll the VM instead.
from vxsdk import VxServerError
try:
    c.deploy.container(image="sebp/elk", ports=["5601:5601"], ...)
except VxServerError as e:
    if "524" in str(e):
        # The deploy is still running on the node; poll `docker ps` on the VM
        # or `c.sessions.list(status="running")` for the new session.
        pass
    else:
        raise
```

Entry class is exported under four interchangeable names (VxCloud / vxcloud / Vxsdk / Client) so it reads naturally from any of the platform's other-language SDKs.
19 modules — every method shipped in 2026.8.17 is documented below with a runnable example.

code_blocks:
npm install @vxcloud/sdk
# or:  pnpm add @vxcloud/sdk
# or:  yarn add @vxcloud/sdk

# All four named exports below alias the SAME class — pick whichever
# import name your team prefers:
#   import { VxCloud } from '@vxcloud/sdk';     // canonical (PascalCase)
#   import { vxcloud } from '@vxcloud/sdk';     // lowercase brand
#   import { Vxsdk }   from '@vxcloud/sdk';     // mirrors Python `vxsdk`
#   import { Client }  from '@vxcloud/sdk';     // mirrors `vxsdk.Client`

deploy (container + 14 stacks) — Deploy any Docker image, or any of the 14 supported stacks (fastapi, react, nextjs, django, nodejs, python, golang, rust, cpp, php, static, angular, vuejs, expo, flask, java, laravel, metaldb). Source is either a pre-built zip Buffer or a git repo URL. Single-command HTTPS via `enableSsl`/`domain`/`sslEmail` — host nginx + certbot for `container`, shared Traefik for stack deploys.
Docker container (HTTPS):
```
// Single call: deploy + cert + nginx vhost.
// Requires grafana.example.com A record -> 13.216.243.13 already set.
const sess = await c.deploy.container({
  image: 'grafana/grafana:latest',
  name:  'grafana',
  ports: ['3000:3000'],
  env:   ['GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD=changeme'],
  restart: 'unless-stopped',
  enableSsl: true,
  domain:    'grafana.example.com',
  sslEmail:  'ops@example.com',
  host: '13.216.243.13', sshUser: 'ubuntu',
  keyPairName: 'AWSPRODKEY1',     // must be in Vault
});
console.log(sess.sessionId, sess.sslCertificateStatus);
```
Vault (dev mode, HTTPS):
```
const sess = await c.deploy.container({
  image:   'hashicorp/vault:latest',
  name:    'vault',
  command: 'server -dev',
  capAdd:  ['IPC_LOCK'],
  env: [
    'VAULT_DEV_ROOT_TOKEN_ID=devroot',
    'VAULT_DEV_LISTEN_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0:8200',
  ],
  ports:    ['8200:8200'],
  enableSsl: true,
  domain:    'vault.example.com',
  sslEmail:  'ops@example.com',
  host: '13.216.243.13', sshUser: 'ubuntu',
  keyPairName: 'AWSPRODKEY1',
});
```
FastAPI from git repo (HTTPS):
```
// Bootstraps shared vxcloud-traefik on the VM + obtains an ACME cert
// via HTTP-01 on :80, then routes Host(api.example.com) -> the nginx sidecar.
const sess = await c.deploy.fastapi({
  repoUrl: 'https://github.com/me/api.git',
  branch:  'main',
  appName: 'studio-backend',
  entry:   'app.app:app',
  requirements: 'requirements.txt',
  appPort: '8000', httpPort: '80',
  enableSsl: true,
  domain:    'api.example.com',
  sslEmail:  'ops@example.com',
  host: '203.0.113.24', sshUser: 'ubuntu',
  keyPairName: 'AWSPRODKEY1',
});
```
React from local build (HTTPS):
```
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';

const zip = readFileSync('./build.zip');

await c.deploy.react({
  zipBundle: { filename: 'build.zip', content: zip },
  appName:   'studio-react3d',
  buildMode: 'production',
  httpPort:  '80',
  enableSsl: true,
  domain:    'app.example.com',
  sslEmail:  'ops@example.com',
  host: '203.0.113.24', sshUser: 'ubuntu',
  keyPairName: 'AWSPRODKEY1',
});
```

Tenant-node CRUD against the VxCloud control plane. The Go SDK mirrors `vxcli node {list,add,update,delete,set-default}` 1:1. Self-hosted (BYO) registration uses POST /api/v1/auth/nodes/self-hosted, partial updates go through PATCH /api/v1/auth/nodes/{id}, deletes via DELETE /api/v1/auth/nodes/{id}.
```
import "github.com/prodxcloud/vxcloud/nodes"

all, _ := c.Nodes().List(ctx)
for _, n := range all {
    fmt.Println(n.ID, n.Label(), n.BaseURL(),
        map[bool]string{true: "DEFAULT", false: ""}[n.IsDefaultNode])
}

def, _ := c.Nodes().Default(ctx)
fmt.Println("default node:", def.Label())

_ = c.Nodes().SetDefault(ctx, def.ID)
```

deploy (container + 14 stacks) — Deploy any Docker image (`Deploy().Container`) or any of the 14 supported stacks (`Deploy().Stack(kind, opts)`). Single-command HTTPS via `EnableSSL`/`Domain`/`SSLEmail` — host nginx + certbot for `Container`, shared Traefik for `Stack`.
Docker container (HTTPS):
```
import (
    "github.com/prodxcloud/vxcloud/deploy"
    "github.com/prodxcloud/vxcloud/install"
)

sess, err := c.Deploy().Container(ctx, deploy.ContainerOpts{
    SSH: install.SSH{
        Host:        "13.216.243.13",
        User:        "ubuntu",
        KeyPairName: "AWSPRODKEY1",   // must be in Vault
    },
    Name:      "grafana",
    Image:     "grafana/grafana:latest",
    Ports:     []string{"3000:3000"},
    Env:       []string{"GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD=changeme"},
    EnableSSL: true,
    Domain:    "grafana.example.com",
    SSLEmail:  "ops@example.com",
})
if err != nil { panic(err) }
fmt.Println(sess.SessionID, sess.AccessURL)
```
Vault (dev mode, HTTPS):
```
sess, err := c.Deploy().Container(ctx, deploy.ContainerOpts{
    SSH:     install.SSH{Host: "h", User: "root", KeyPairName: "VPS1"},
    Name:    "vault",
    Image:   "hashicorp/vault:latest",
    Command: "server -dev",        // safe: no commas
    CapAdd:  []string{"IPC_LOCK"},
    Env: []string{
        "VAULT_DEV_ROOT_TOKEN_ID=devroot",
        "VAULT_DEV_LISTEN_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0:8200",
    },
    Ports:     []string{"8200:8200"},
    EnableSSL: true,
    Domain:    "vault.example.com",
    SSLEmail:  "ops@example.com",
})
```
PostgreSQL (DB on :5432; HTTPS 502):
```
// Postgres is a TCP service — HTTPS nginx in front 502s (HTTP nginx
// can't speak postgres). Use psql -h db.example.com -p 5432 directly.
sess, err := c.Deploy().Container(ctx, deploy.ContainerOpts{
    SSH:   install.SSH{Host: "h", User: "root", KeyPairName: "VPS1"},
    Name:  "postgres",
    Image: "postgres:16",
    Env: []string{
        "POSTGRES_PASSWORD=changeme",
        "POSTGRES_USER=app",
        "POSTGRES_DB=app",
    },
    Ports:     []string{"5432:5432"},
    EnableSSL: true,
    Domain:    "db.example.com",
    SSLEmail:  "ops@example.com",
})
```

Fine-tune a base model + Wait for completion:
```
job, _ := ac.FineTuning().Create(ctx, map[string]interface{}{
    "name":          "support-tone-v1",
    "base_model":    "claude-haiku-4-5",
    "training_file": "ds-abc123",
    "epochs":        3,
})
done, err := ac.FineTuning().Wait(ctx, job["id"].(string), agentcontrol.WaitOptions{
    Timeout:  time.Hour,
    Interval: 10 * time.Second,
    OnTick:   func(j agentcontrol.Result) { fmt.Println("status:", j["status"]) },
})
if err != nil { panic(err) }
fmt.Println("final:", done["status"], "· model:", done["model_id"])
```
Training extras — Clone, Restart, Logs, Metrics, Chat:
```
tr := ac.Training()
_, _   = tr.Restart(ctx, "tj_abc")
clone, _ := tr.Clone(ctx, "tj_abc")
fmt.Println("cloned:", clone["id"])

logs, _    := tr.Logs(ctx, "tj_abc")
metrics, _ := tr.Metrics(ctx, "tj_abc")
fmt.Println("last epoch:", metrics["epochs"])

reply, _ := tr.Chat(ctx, "tj_abc", agentcontrol.TrainingChatRequest{

chunks.text:
Manage VxCloud workspaces, credentials, VMs, databases, deploys, and Kubernetes clusters as Terraform-native resources. Full import support; state diffs against the live platform.
7 modules — every method shipped in v1.0.0-beta3 is documented below with a runnable example.

- Provider configuration — 1 example
- Cloud credentials — 1 example
- VMs — 1 example
- Databases — 1 example
- Application deploys — 1 example
- Kubernetes — 1 example
- Importing existing resources — 1 example

The provider authenticates with an API key; workspace_id is optional and inferred from the key by default.
```
provider "VxCloud" {
  api_key   = var.VxCloud_api_key
  workspace = var.workspace_id          # optional
  # node_url = "https://node1.vxcloud.io"  # override active node
}
```

Postgres / MySQL / MongoDB managed databases.:
```
resource "VxCloud_database" "app_db" {
  provider       = "aws"
  engine         = "postgresql"
  instance_class = "db.t3.medium"
  storage_gb     = 100
  depends_on     = [VxCloud_aws_credentials.main]
}

output "db_url" { value = VxCloud_database.app_db.connection_string }
```

Deploy applications onto a previously-provisioned VM. Same surface as the SDK's deploy module — exposed as a Terraform resource for declarative state.
```
resource "VxCloud_deploy_fastapi" "api" {
  source_dir      = "./"
  app_name        = "studio-backend"
  entry           = "app.app:app"
  requirements    = "requirements.txt"
  app_port        = 8000
  http_port       = 80
  host            = VxCloud_vm.api.public_ip
  ssh_user        = "ubuntu"
  key_pair_name   = "AWSPRODKEY1.PEM"

  env_vars = {
    DATABASE_URL = VxCloud_database.app_db.connection_string
  }

  depends_on = [VxCloud_vm.api, VxCloud_database.app_db]
}
```

chunks.page_title: Deploy a Next.js application from GitHub
chunks.text: The Next.js wizard lives at Dashboard → Development → Next.js Application. Every wizard in the Development tab shares the same shape: pick a target node, fill four steps, click Deploy, watch the live progress.

chunks.page_title: Deploy a Next.js application from GitHub
chunks.text: In the dashboard sidebar, click Development → tab "Development" → card "Next.js Application" → button "Deploy". The card shows the Next.js logo and a short description. Clicking Deploy opens the four-step wizard with a node selector pinned to the top right.

chunks.page_title: Deploy a Next.js application from GitHub
chunks.text:
Pick a Deployment Type (Virtual Machine, Kubernetes, or Docker Host). Enter the Server IP of your target VM, the SSH Username (typically ubuntu), and pick an SSH Key Pair Name from the dropdown — it lists every keypair stored in your workspace Vault.
- ▸ Use Test SSH Connection (green button) to verify reachability before continuing.
- ▸ The Services Checking button (yellow) runs runtime smoke-tests on the VM if you want a deeper preflight.

chunks.page_title: Deploy a Next.js application from GitHub
chunks.text: Choose "From Repository" (default) or "Upload Zip". For Git: paste the repo URL, set a branch (defaults to main), pick the Git provider (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket), and either OAuth-connect or paste a personal access token. The token is stored in your workspace Vault and reused on subsequent deploys — you only enter it once.

chunks.page_title: Deploy a Next.js application from GitHub
chunks.text: Select Build Mode (production / development), Node.js Version (22, 20, 18, or 16), and an App Name. App Name is what you will see later in Monitoring as the resource identifier.

chunks.page_title: Deploy a Next.js application from GitHub
chunks.text: Set Entry Point (default ".") and Package File ("package.json"). Add Environment Variables — one KEY=value per line. Set Application Port (typically 3000), HTTP Port (80) and HTTPS Port (443) for the front-facing reverse proxy.

chunks.page_title: Deploy a Next.js application from GitHub
chunks.text:
A live progress card appears: 10% session created → 38% repo cloned → 50% npm install → 70% next build → 90% systemd unit started → 100% reverse proxy live. Logs stream over WebSocket; the same view is reachable later under Monitoring → session ID.
Stuck halfway through? Email [email protected] — most replies land within an hour during weekdays.
Was this page helpful?

chunks.page_title: Deploy a FastAPI service with managed Postg…
chunks.text: You will visit two wizards: Databases → MetalDB to provision Postgres, then Development → FastAPI to deploy the app pointing at that database.

chunks.page_title: Deploy a FastAPI service with managed Postg…
chunks.text:
Dashboard → Databases → tab "Cloud" → MetalDB card → Deploy. The wizard collects: Target VM Hostname/IP, SSH Username, SSH Key Pair, Database Name, Database User, Database Password, port (default 5432), Postgres Version, and optional replication / backup toggles.
- ▸ Use the Test SSH Connection button before clicking Deploy.
- ▸ Enable Backup if this is anything other than a throwaway demo — VxCloud will write nightly backups to the same VM (or to S3 if configured).

chunks.page_title: Deploy a FastAPI service with managed Postg…
heading_path: Wait for MetalDB to come up
chunks.text: The progress bar walks: 10% session start → 40% terraform apply → 70% Postgres systemd unit running → 90% admin role created → 100% connection details written to Vault. The dashboard shows the connection string and pgAdmin URL when ready.

chunks.page_title: Deploy a FastAPI service with managed Postg…
chunks.text: Dashboard → Development → FastAPI Application → Deploy. Step 1 (Server Configuration) is identical to the Next.js flow — pick the same VM you put MetalDB on, or a different VM that can reach it on port 5432.

chunks.page_title: Deploy a FastAPI service with managed Postg…
chunks.text: Paste your FastAPI repo URL. The wizard expects a project with requirements.txt or pyproject.toml at the root and an entry point exposing FastAPI() — the conventional `main.py` with `app = FastAPI()`.

chunks.page_title: Deploy a FastAPI service with managed Postg…
chunks.text: Set App Name, Python Version (3.12 / 3.11 / 3.10), and worker count for uvicorn/gunicorn. The wizard enables --workers automatically based on the chosen CPU count.

chunks.page_title: Deploy a FastAPI service with managed Postg…
chunks.text:
Set App Port (8000), Entry Point (`main.py:app`), Requirements File (`requirements.txt`). In Environment Variables, paste:

DATABASE_URL=postgres://<dbuser>:<dbpass>@<vm-ip>:5432/<dbname>

Use the credentials Vault wrote when MetalDB came up — the dashboard surfaces them as a copy button on the MetalDB resource page.

chunks.page_title: Deploy a FastAPI service with managed Postg…
chunks.text:
Hit Deploy. After ~3 minutes you will see the API live at http://<vm-ip>:8000/docs (FastAPI auto-docs). The Monitoring tab shows both resources — MetalDB and the FastAPI service — linked under the same workspace.
Stuck halfway through? Email [email protected] — most replies land within an hour during weekdays.
Was this page helpful?

chunks.page_title: Deploy any Docker Compose stack with the Cu…
chunks.text: Open Dashboard → Development → "Custom Compose Stack" → Deploy. Four steps: server, stack metadata, compose definition, review.

chunks.page_title: Deploy any Docker Compose stack with the Cu…
chunks.text: Same as every wizard: pick a target VM and Vault keypair. Test SSH Connection.

chunks.page_title: Deploy any Docker Compose stack with the Cu…
chunks.text: Pick a Stack Name (lowercase, alphanumeric + hyphens — used as the directory name on the VM) and a Cloud Provider tag for the audit log. Optionally point at a private Docker registry — VxCloud resolves credentials from Vault and runs docker login during the deploy.

chunks.page_title: Deploy any Docker Compose stack with the Cu…
chunks.text:
Click the Templates dropdown to pick from 20 starters: Postgres + pgAdmin, Monitoring (Grafana + Prometheus), Nginx, Vault + Consul (dev), Ollama + Open WebUI, LAMP, MEAN, WordPress, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis, RabbitMQ, Kafka (KRaft), Elasticsearch + Kibana, Jenkins, Gitea, Portainer, Mattermost, n8n, Keycloak. Each template is a self-contained YAML — pick one, edit anything, and click Validate.
- ▸ The Validate button parses the YAML and confirms a `services:` key exists.
- ▸ Templates use `$${VAR}` (escaped) so docker-compose does the substitution at runtime, not the wizard.
- ▸ Generate with AI uses the same chat backend to scaffold a new stack from a description.

chunks.page_title: Deploy any Docker Compose stack with the Cu…
chunks.text:
Confirm the summary. Hit Deploy. The progress feed walks: 10% session start → 30% Vault credentials resolved → 50% files SCP'd to /opt/compose/<stack>/ → 70% docker compose pull → 90% docker compose up -d → 100% docker compose ps shows expected containers.
Stuck halfway through? Email [email protected] — most replies land within an hour during weekdays.
Was this page helpful?

chunks.page_title: Build a CI/CD pipeline with blue-green depl…
chunks.text: Dashboard → CI/CD → "New Pipeline". You build the pipeline as a sequence of stages; each stage is a vxcli deploy invocation under the hood, with environment-specific configuration.

chunks.page_title: Build a CI/CD pipeline with blue-green depl…
chunks.text: Name the pipeline (e.g. "my-api-pipeline"), point at the source repo, and pick a trigger — push to a branch, tag, or manual.

chunks.page_title: Build a CI/CD pipeline with blue-green depl…
chunks.text: The Build stage runs your CI step (npm test, pytest, go test, etc.) inside a fresh container. Cache is keyed by lockfile hash. If tests fail, the pipeline halts before any deployment.

chunks.page_title: Build a CI/CD pipeline with blue-green depl…
chunks.text: The Deploy → Staging stage uses the same Development wizard config you used for the original deploy, but in environment="staging". Traffic is automatic — staging gets all of it.

chunks.page_title: Build a CI/CD pipeline with blue-green depl…
chunks.text: Before production, drop in an Approval gate. The pipeline pauses; whoever has the role "Production Deployer" gets a Slack/email ping with a one-click Approve button. Audit log records who clicked.

chunks.page_title: Build a CI/CD pipeline with blue-green depl…
chunks.text: In the Production stage, toggle Strategy = Blue-Green. VxCloud spins up the new version on parallel infrastructure, runs the configured smoke-test, then atomically switches the load balancer. Old version stays warm for 15 minutes for instant rollback.

chunks.page_title: Build a CI/CD pipeline with blue-green depl…
chunks.text: A push to the configured branch fires the pipeline. The pipeline view shows each stage as it runs with live logs. On any failure, the pipeline halts and pings the configured channel.

chunks.page_title: Build a CI/CD pipeline with blue-green depl…
chunks.text:
On the Production stage card, every successful past deploy has a "Rollback to this" button. Click → traffic flips back in seconds → audit log records the rollback.
Stuck halfway through? Email [email protected] — most replies land within an hour during weekdays.
Was this page helpful?

chunks.page_title: Store and rotate cloud credentials with Vau…
chunks.text: Dashboard → Settings → Vault. The page lists every credential currently registered in your workspace, grouped by category (Cloud Providers, Git, Docker Registries, SSH Keys, Custom).

chunks.page_title: Store and rotate cloud credentials with Vau…

chunks.page_title: AI Models: One API for Every Model
heading_path: Inference, streaming, and evals — without vendor lock-in
chunks.text:
Same call shape across every provider. Built-in fallback when a model is slow or rate-limited. Continuous evaluation in CI so you only ship a model swap when the goldens still pass.
- Per-request cost, latency, and token telemetry — automatic
- BYO keys: Anthropic, OpenAI, Bedrock, Azure, Vertex, vLLM
- Eval suites block model promotion if regressions appear
- OpenTelemetry traces span model + tools + your app code
```
# pip install vxcloud-ai
from vxcloud.ai import Client

client = Client()  # picks up VX_API_KEY from env

# 1) Inference — same call shape across every provider.
resp = client.complete(
    model="claude-opus-4-7",
    fallback=["claude-sonnet-4-6", "gpt-reasoning"],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Refactor this function for testability."}],
    max_tokens=2048,
    metadata={"workspace": "studio", "session": "ide-42"},
)
print(resp.text)
print(resp.usage, resp.cost_usd, resp.latency_ms)

# 2) Streaming with cancellation.
with client.stream(model="claude-sonnet-4-6", messages=[...]) as s:
    for token in s:
        print(token, end="", flush=True)

# 3) Evals — score a model against your own golden set.
report = client.evals.run(
    model="claude-haiku-4-5",
    suite="support/intent-classification",
    parallelism=8,
)
print(report.summary())  # accuracy, p50/p95 latency, $/req
```

Post structured CI/deploy/incident events from any service. Spawn AI copilots scoped to a room. Subscribe to AI suggestions and gate them behind your existing approvals.
- vxcli chat — multi-provider, multi-session, terminal-native

```
# Multi-provider AI chat in your terminal — no GUI required.
# Switch providers and models mid-session; sessions persist locally.

vxcli chat \
  --provider anthropic \
  --model    claude-opus-4-7

# Slash commands inside the session
/sessions             # picker for prior conversations
/model haiku          # hot-swap to claude-haiku-4-5
/provider openai      # hot-swap provider
/files add ./PR-491.diff   # ground the next answer in a file
/export markdown ./out.md  # dump the transcript to disk

# Pipe-friendly: read stdin, emit answer to stdout.
git log --oneline -20 | vxcli chat --stdin --one-shot \
  "summarise these commits as release notes"

# Use it in CI: post the digest into a chat room.
vxcli chat --one-shot "weekly perf summary from $(date -d '7 days ago')" \
  | vxcli rooms post --channel '#weekly-ops'
```

chunks.page_title: Virtual Machines on 8 Clouds, One CLI
heading_path: Same shape across every cloud — no provider-specific quirks
chunks.text:
Choose the surface that fits the moment: a quick CLI to spin up a one-off, Terraform for durable infrastructure, REST for in-app provisioning. Drift detection and signed images are on by default for all three.
- Idempotent operations — re-run the same command safely
- Drift detection across cloud accounts in one dashboard
- Signed cloud-init scripts and image attestations on every boot
- Snapshots, resize, and migration without losing the data volume
```
# Provision a VM in any cloud, in any region — same flags everywhere.
vxcli vm create vm-api-01 \
  --cloud   aws          \
  --region  us-east-1    \
  --type    g3.medium    \
  --image   ubuntu-22.04 \
  --disk    160          \
  --ssh-key team-prod    \
  --userdata ./cloud-init.yml

# → Provisioning… 13.7s
# → ssh [email protected]
# → cost: $0.084/hr · $60.48/mo

# Snapshot before risky migration
vxcli vm snapshot vm-api-01 --label "pre-migration-2026-05-10"

# Resize without losing data
vxcli vm resize vm-api-01 --type c5.xlarge --downtime-ok

# Burst into spot capacity for batch
vxcli vm create-batch ml-train --type gpu.l4 --count 12 --spot --max-price 0.40
```
Pick the right size from a goal
vxcli vm suggest "Postgres 14, 200GB hot data, 1k QPS" — recommends r5.2xlarge with disk + alerts.
Production-grade by default

heading_path: Common challenges — and how we solve them
chunks.text:
Challenge
Cluster sprawl: dev, staging, regional, and customer-dedicated clusters multiply faster than the platform team can keep them upgraded.
How VxCloud solves it
One management plane shows every cluster, its Kubernetes version, drift from policy baselines, and a click-to-upgrade path with rolling node-pool replacement.
Challenge
Autoscaling fights itself — HPA, cluster-autoscaler, and Karpenter conflict and produce thrashing or unschedulable pods.
How VxCloud solves it
Pre-tuned autoscaling profiles per workload class (web, batch, GPU, stateful) with circuit breakers that stabilize node churn during bursts.
Challenge
Day-2 operations — upgrades, etcd backups, certificate rotation — eat the platform team’s sprint capacity.
How VxCloud solves it
Managed control plane handles upgrades, etcd snapshots, certificate rotation, and CVE patching on a published cadence with maintenance windows you control.
Challenge
Security teams cannot prove what is running where, or whether a CVE has been remediated across every cluster and namespace.
How VxCloud solves it
Continuous SBOM and CVE scanning per image, per cluster, per namespace, with one-click remediation tickets and audit trail for compliance evidence.

heading_path: Build the next workflow on top of Backup & Restore
chunks.text: Start in minutes with VxCloud-managed infrastructure, AI-assisted setup, and a production-ready baseline your team can extend safely.

One API for the whole funnel
333 SalesShift operations and 57 messaging and call operations across 312 paths, from contact creation to a countersigned PDF.
Your domain, your data
Mail leaves under your own sending identity and your records stay in your workspace. Sending and enrichment run on our infrastructure or on credentials you supply — which of the two is your plan's, and the API is the same either way. AI is always the second kind: it runs on a key you connect.
Documented against a live service
121 of these endpoints were called against a running server while this reference was written. The rest say so, plainly.

Worth reading before the quickstart, because it decides what some of these calls will answer. There are four plans: three paid, and a 7-day free trial that every workspace starts on. All four run on infrastructure VxCloud operates — the relay the mail leaves from, the prospect data, the models behind the assistant and the machines under all three. What separates them is volume, and going past a plan's included volume is metered rather than blocked.
The trial is a clock, not a tier. When it runs out managed.sending , managed.ai and managed.compute all go false together and the three metered allowances go to zero — reads keep working and nothing is deleted, but the paths that cost us money answer 402. Check trial.expired to tell that state apart from a plan that simply does not include a capability.
Plan
Per user, per month
Where it runs
Free trial
$0
The whole platform for 7 days, no card. 2,000 emails, 500 reveals, 200 AI credits, 3 users — totals for the week, not monthly.
Starter
$14
Our relay, prospect data and assistant, with three sending identities. 5,000 emails, 1,000 reveals and 500 AI credits a month.
Professional
$39
The same, with more volume, mailbox rotation, workflow automation and API access.
Organization
$89
The same, uncapped sending, on dedicated infrastructure in the region you choose.
Allowances on the paid plans are per seat and pool across the workspace, so a number you read back is the per-seat quota multiplied by the seats you bought. The trial is a flat workspace allowance instead — there are no seats to multiply — and it is the only plan with a user ceiling, at three.
Past a plan's allowance, usage is metered rather than refused: $1.00 per 1,000 emails, $2.00 per 100 prospect reveals, $0.02 per call minute and $10.00 per additional node per month. Those four are the only metered resources — nothing else in the product has a counter on it.

One credit is one request to the assistant. Three things to know before you build against it:
Two buckets, and only one of them resets
The plan's monthly allowance is spent first and resets on the 1st (UTC); purchased packs are spent second and never expire. GET /billing/credits returns both separately — included_remaining and purchased_balance — plus total_remaining. A null allowance means unlimited, matching the plans API; rendering it as 0 is the one mistake to avoid.
Top-ups are one-time purchases, not a subscription
POST /billing/credits/checkout with a pack_code returns a Stripe Checkout URL in payment mode. Packs are 1,000 for $10, 5,000 for $45 and 10,000 for $80. Credits land on /billing/credits/confirm or the webhook, whichever arrives first — both use the same idempotency ref, so a pack cannot be credited twice.
Your own key spends nothing
Connect a model key under Settings → Integrations and the assistant uses it instead of ours. Those requests are not metered at all: credits.metered reads false and the balance does not move. You pay your provider directly, at their rate, with nothing added by us.
allowance.ai on /billing/entitlements is the plan's monthly INCLUDED figure and nothing more. It does not know about purchased packs and it does not know what has been spent this month, so it is the wrong field to render as a balance — /billing/credits is the one that answers that. On the trial it reads 0 , which is correct and is not a lock-out: the trial's 200 credits are granted once into the purchased bucket at activation rather than allowanced monthly, because a monthly allowance on a seven-day plan is a contradiction.
All three managed.* flags are load-bearing now. They read true on every plan in the catalogue and go false together when a trial expires, so a client should branch on them rather than on a price of zero or a quota of zero.

It is not a bug and not a permission problem, and the detail string is written to be shown to the user unchanged. Creating a contact past the stored-contact cap, importing a CSV past it, converting pool rows in bulk and inviting a teammate past the user ceiling all raise it.

A client that collapses 402 into 403 loses the difference between “upgrade” and “you may not” — see the API conventions for the rest of the status vocabulary.

An organization can put its own accounts behind any capability, and we take no margin on usage billed to them. It is a preference on every plan rather than a requirement of any: sending, enrichment and the assistant all have a managed default, and connecting your own account replaces it and stops that usage drawing on your allowance. The table below states what each capability does when nothing is connected — which depends on the plan, so GET /billing/entitlements is the call to make before you assume a row applies to you:
You connect

Sending, reply detection, the webmail surface

Without it — an expired trial, or a workspace that has opted into its own node — the send is refused rather than queued: 200 with success false, a tracking row at status 'failed', provider 'refused', and the reason in 'error'. Invoice checkout, payments and subscriptions

Connected providers for the calling organization are listed by GET /settings/integrations . The AI row above is not hypothetical: the organization these docs were written against has three email integrations and no AI provider, which is exactly why call transcription is marked unproven throughout.
Stripe cannot be connected today
The 400 above tells you to connect Stripe under Settings → Integrations. That instruction cannot currently be followed, and it is the server's wording rather than a description of something that works. Settings → Integrations has four groups — email, AI, SMS and enrichment — and no payments group; and the API refuses the connection outright:

chunks.text:
REST API reference
All 390 operations, grouped by domain, with parameters, error cases and a copyable curl for each.
vxcli
The command-line surface — the fastest way to try a call without writing a client.
SDKs
Python, TypeScript, Go, C++ and Java clients, and an honest map of which endpoints each one covers.
Guides
Task-shaped walkthroughs: plans and self-hosting, sending, deliverability, sequences, leads, contracts, quotes, calendar and webhooks.

The reference is generated from an inventory of the running service, and each endpoint states how much is known about it. Nothing is described as working because it looks like it should.
- live-call Called against http://127.0.0.1:8741 during this inventory run; the `verified` block holds the request and the response.
- session-verified The feature was verified working against the live system in the session that produced this inventory, but this specific route was not re-called here.
- code-only Read in source for this inventory and not executed. Undemonstrated is not the same as broken — but do not write it up as proven.
- known-unproven One of the two items in known_unproven.
Two capabilities are fully built and still unproven here — OAuth mailbox connect, and call transcription. Both are called out where they appear, with what was actually observed. See the API conventions for the full statements.

Two prefixes cover everything here: /api/v1/salesshift for the 333 SalesShift operations, and /api/v1/messaging for the 57 messaging and call operations. Examples use https://api.vxcloud.io because that is the host every verified call on these pages was made against.
There is no OpenAPI document. app.py constructs FastAPI with docs_url=None, redoc_url=None and openapi_url=None, so /openapi.json and /docs are 404 on the running service. Do not tell readers to browse them.

Every endpoint names the dependency that guards it. There are three, and they accept different credentials:
Dependency
Routes
Accepts
Scope
get_org_user
296
Authorization: Bearer <jwt> X-API-Key: xc_<env>_...
Resolves both a user and an organization; every query is filtered by that organization_id. On failure: 401 {"detail": "Not authenticated — provide Bearer token or X-API-Key"} (observed live).
get_current_user
6
Authorization: Bearer <jwt>
Platform JWT; no organization scoping applied by the dependency.
get_current_user_id
46
Authorization: Bearer <jwt>
Caller's user id only; room membership is enforced by _require_member inside each handler. On failure: 401 {"detail": "Not authenticated"} (observed live).
route.auth carries {required, dependency, scope}. The accepted credentials and the exact failure body for each dependency live once, below, under auth_dependencies — look the dependency name up there. The `authorization` and `X-API-Key` headers are deliberately absent from route.params: FastAPI lists them because get_org_user declares them as Header() params, but they are the credential, not an option.
API keys are accepted with the prefixes xc_dev_, xc_live_, xc_test_, xc_stg_, xc_sbx_, xc_prev_ . The 46 messaging routes take a Bearer JWT only.
31 endpoints carry no auth dependency — and they are not one list
Do NOT describe these as 'public' as a group. Only the `open` ones take no credential at all; the rest carry the credential somewhere other than an Authorization header, and two of them do a full auth check inside the handler.
- open 1 No credential of any kind.
- in-handler-auth 2 A normal credential, resolved by the handler rather than by a Depends(). These are authenticated routes.
- signature-verified 2 Anonymous caller, but the request body is verified against a stored provider secret.
- url-secret-only 17 The token, slug or id in the URL is the ONLY credential. Treat those URLs as secrets.
- public-by-design 9 Meant to be reachable by anyone — published pages, the tracking pixel, and the unsubscribe flow.

There is no single wrapper. Each endpoint states which of these it uses, so read that line before writing a client against it.
success+data 159
{success: true, data: ...}, optionally with `pagination`.
success+custom 115
Has `success`, but the payload is under other keys too — e.g. {success, contact, messages} or {success, data, recipients}.
bare-model 12
The Pydantic response_model serialised directly. No `success`, no `data` — the model's fields are the top level.
bare-object 73
A plain object or array with no envelope, built by the handler or a helper.
html 9
text/html — including the error responses.
binary 9
A file or image body (PDF, ICS, PNG, attachment, raw message source).
text 1
text/plain (the CSV report export).
redirect 2
A 3xx redirect rather than a body.
empty 1
Returns None — a 200 with a null JSON body.
sse 1

Failures are FastAPI's standard shape — an HTTP status and a detail string. Each endpoint lists the ones its own handler raises; where the message is computed, the expression is shown rather than a made-up sample.
```
{
  "detail": "Not authenticated — provide Bearer token or X-API-Key"
}
```
The statuses that carry a distinct meaning across the whole API, rather than one endpoint's own validation:
Status
What it means here
401
No credential, or one the server could not verify. Nothing about the request body was looked at.
402
A plan refusal: the operation would spend something this plan does not include. It is never softened to 403, because the two need different UI — one offers an upgrade, the other does not. The detail string names the plan, the ceiling and the current number and is written to be shown to a user unchanged.
403
A permission or ownership problem — the credential is valid and the answer is still no. Registering a node that identifies as somebody else's workspace is the clearest example.
404
No such row, or no such row in your workspace. The two are deliberately indistinguishable.
409
A duplicate, or a state conflict: the request is well-formed but the workspace is not in a state where it makes sense. POST /billing/activate answers 409 when a live plan would be downgraded.
410
A pool record erased at the person's request. Terminal and global — not an outage, and retrying will never succeed.
503
A capability this deployment does not have configured. Every Stripe-touching billing route answers it when no Stripe key is present.
Where a 402 comes from is answerable in one call: GET /api/v1/salesshift/billing/entitlements returns the resolved plan and every allowance; Plans and self-hosting lists the five places in the product that raise it.

Two paths report a refusal inside a 200 body instead of raising, because both run in loops over many rows and one refused row must not fail the batch. POST /api/v1/salesshift/email/send answers 200 with status: "failed" and provider: "refused" , the reason in error ; POST /api/v1/salesshift/ai/write-email answers 200 with source: "template" and the reason in reason . A client that reads only the status code will record both as successes.

- live-call Called against http://127.0.0.1:8741 during this inventory run; the `verified` block holds the request and the response.
- session-verified The feature was verified working against the live system in the session that produced this inventory, but this specific route was not re-called here.
- code-only Read in source for this inventory and not executed. Undemonstrated is not the same as broken — but do not write it up as proven.
- known-unproven One of the two items in known_unproven.
Do not upgrade a `code-only` route to a worked example in a doc. Either call it first and update this file, or write it as a reference entry without an 'it works like this' claim.

oauth-mailbox-connect
OAuth mailbox connect is fully built — PKCE, Vault-stored tokens, XOAUTH2 and refresh — and a real send completes AUTH XOAUTH2 -> 250 queued. No Microsoft or Google mailbox has ever consented here, so the final SMTP hop to a real provider is UNPROVEN.
What was actually observed: GET /webmail/oauth/providers returned 200 with configured=true and missing=[] for both microsoft and google, and one account in this org carries auth_method=oauth / oauth_provider=microsoft with oauth_connected_at set. That is client configuration and a local proof account, not consent from a real provider mailbox.
GET /api/v1/salesshift/webmail/oauth/providers POST /api/v1/salesshift/webmail/oauth/{provider}/connect POST /api/v1/salesshift/webmail/accounts/{account_id}/reconnect GET /api/v1/salesshift/webmail/oauth/callback
call-transcription-summary
Call transcription and summary have never run with real data. No org has an AI provider key, so every recording ends at status='unavailable'.
What was actually observed: GET /settings/integrations for the test org returned three integrations, all integration_type='email' (imap, smtp, smtp). There is no integration_type='ai' row, which is the condition that leaves transcription unavailable.

Explainable verification of any address: syntax, domain, MX, mail provider, disposable and role checks, SPF/DMARC, a live SMTP dialogue with the mail server, and a catch-all canary. Each check prints the moment the server finishes it. The probe stops at RCPT TO , so no message is ever created, but it does talk to real mail servers, which is why the server meters it.
12 a minute, 150 an hour

Verify one or more addresses and explain the verdict: verified, risky, not_verified or inconclusive, with a 0-100 score and an A-F grade.
Calls
POST {vxcloud} /api/v1/salesshift/verifier/stream (SSE: one step event per check, then result ) · POST {vxcloud} /api/v1/salesshift/verifier/check with --json or --no-stream
Arguments
One or more addresses. Duplicates (case-insensitive) are checked once.
Flag
Type
Default
What it does
--file
string
""
One address per line; blank lines and lines starting with # are skipped. Capped at 150. Ends with a summary table: email, verdict, score, detail.
--json
bool
false

vxcli --no-color salesshift verify [email protected]
```

```
  ▎ [email protected]  ───────────────────────────────────────
    ✓  Address format             Well-formed address that SMTP can carry.
    ✓  Domain exists              outlook.com is registered and resolves.  12ms
    ✓  Mail servers (MX)          1 mail server published; mail goes to outlook-com.olc.protection.outlook.com first.
    ·  Mail provider              Outlook.com (Microsoft consumer) hosts this mailbox (a personal account).
    ✓  Disposable & role check    Not a throwaway service and not a shared role address.
    ✓  Domain authentication      Publishes SPF and DMARC — a maintained mail domain.  26ms
    ✓  Live mailbox check (SMTP)  The mail server confirmed this exact mailbox exists.  6426ms
    ✓  Catch-all test             A made-up address at this domain was rejected, so the server's yes is specific to this mailbox.

    Verdict            VERIFIED  97/100 · A
    Headline           Deliverable — this mailbox exists and accepts mail.
    Detail             mailbox_accepted
    Mail server        outlook-com.olc.protection.outlook.com  via egress node 51.79.205.88
    Took               6.5 s

    Why
      • [email protected] is a well-formed address and outlook.com publishes working mail servers.
      • The Outlook.com (Microsoft consumer) mail server (outlook-com.olc.protection.outlook.com) was asked directly about this mailbox and answered “250 2.1.5 Recipient OK”.
      • It rejected a random address at outlook.com (“550 5.5.0 Requested action not taken: mailbox unavailable (S2017062302). [CH2PEPF00000147.namprd02.prod.outlook.com 2026-10-20T16:47:46.316Z 08DF2EAB4E6771F6]”), so it does not accept everything — the yes is specific to this mailbox.
      • It is a personal mailbox at a consumer provider: real and reachable, though not a company address.
      • outlook.com publishes SPF and DMARC (policy p=none), a sign of a maintained mail domain.
      • No email was sent: the check stops at RCPT TO, before any message is created.
```

chunks.text:
The pool is global and lives on the control plane, not your node. Three rules run through every command here, and each is enforced in the output rather than left to the reader:
- A lead is not mailable. Nothing in this group can email anybody. leads convert and its two bulk forms are the only route to a Contact, and they are where consent metadata is written.
- A mask is not an address. An unrevealed row renders as s•••@kestreldata.example (masked — not revealed) and is labelled every time. has_email says an address exists; email_revealed says you may see it.
- Reveal spends metered quota. Every spending path prints the cost before acting and needs --yes , or an interactive y/N . A pipe or a CI job that cannot answer counts as no.

heading_path: Billing — the plan and the free tier
chunks.text:
What this workspace pays SalesShift. Not to be confused with quotes , invoices and subscriptions , which are money your customers pay you .
Twelve commands. The nine Stripe-facing ones — plans , subscription , invoices , events , checkout , portal , change , cancel , resume — are in the generated reference with their exact flags. The three below exist because “what am I paying for” and “what am I allowed to do right now” are different questions: a trial has a clock on it, an allowance runs out mid-month, and a workspace can point a capability at its own account and stop being metered for it.

heading_path: Billing — the plan and the free tier

Calls

Arguments
None. Aliased self-hosted . This is a command that also has subcommands, so --help shows two usage lines.

  A node must report this workspace id before it can be registered:

```
The TENANT_ID block prints whether or not this plan needs a node. It is the one fact an operator cannot read off the box itself, and the answer to “which id does this workspace expect?” should not depend on what the workspace is paying today.
A workspace name is sometimes accepted as well — real nodes are provisioned with TENANT_ID=<name> — but only when that name is unique across every organization. When it is not, the command prints just the UUID, and the name is refused. That is the case above: three organizations share the name joelwembo , so the also accepted line is absent.

heading_path: Billing — the plan and the free tier
chunks.text:
Register a node, once it has proved which workspace it belongs to. The control plane calls the node — you are not typing a hostname into a text field.
Calls
POST {vxcloud}/api/v1/salesshift/billing/self-hosted/node
Arguments
Exactly one: the base URL of the node. HTTPS is required; http:// is accepted only for localhost and 127.0.0.1 .
No flags.
The server fetches <host>/health and requires the answer to report this workspace’s tenant id. Only then is the host written down, together with the verification time and a fingerprint of <claimed-id>@<version> .
This command deliberately does not use the group’s shared error printer. Each failure needs a different next action, and ✗ HTTP 403 — <detail> on one line buries the tenant id the operator now has to go and set on the box.
```
$ vxcli --no-color salesshift billing node register node1.vxcloud.io

  Not registered — the node did not prove it belongs to this workspace.
  That node identifies as another workspace. Set TENANT_ID=92efb9b0-6785-468a-80d7-ceb5df400168 in its environment and restart it. (Your workspace name 'joelwembo' is shared with another workspace, so only the id above is accepted here.)
  Nothing was recorded, and the node itself was not modified.
exit 1

$ vxcli --no-color salesshift billing node register http://leads.example.com

  Refused — the node did not identify a tenant, or the address is not HTTPS.
  The node must be reachable over HTTPS.
exit 1

$ vxcli --no-color salesshift billing node register https://nope.invalid-host-for-test.io

  The node did not answer.
  Could not reach https://nope.invalid-host-for-test.io/health — HTTPSConnectionPool(host='nope.invalid-host-for-test.io', port=443): Max retries exceeded with url: /health (Caused by NameResolutionError("…Failed to resolve…"))
  It has to be reachable from the control plane, not only from your laptop.
exit 1
```
Running billing node again afterwards showed the workspace still unregistered, which is the point: a refused registration records nothing and does not touch the node either.

Move this workspace onto a free plan. No card, no Stripe, no $0 price object.
Calls
POST {vxcloud}/api/v1/salesshift/billing/activate
Flag
Type
Default
What it does
--plan
string
"self_hosted"
Free plan code to activate. Only plans flagged free are accepted — a paid code is refused here rather than quietly granted.
It also refuses to downgrade a live plan that is paid or granted. That has to go through billing cancel , which tells Stripe when there is a Stripe to tell — losing a plan by accident hurts the same whether it was bought or given.
On success it prints the new plan and, when that plan needs a node and none is registered, the one line that matters next: This plan runs on your own node — nothing sends until one is registered.
The counterpart refusals

Two exit codes. 0 on success, 1 on any failure — including a client-side refusal that never reached the network. The exception is verify , which uses 0 – 3 so a script can tell a bounce from an error — see its exit codes .
A mistyped subcommand exits 0
The leads commands map status codes to sentences rather than echoing “HTTP 402”. Two of those mappings exist because the wrong reaction is expensive: a 402 is a refusal that charged you nothing, and a 410 is terminal rather than an outage to retry.
Status
What the CLI prints
What it means
402
✗ reveal allowance spent — nothing was charged for this attempt.
The meter is empty. Nothing was billed. It also prints Meter: vxcli salesshift leads quota .
410
✗ removed at the person's request.
Terminal. Retrying will not bring it back — the command says so explicitly.
404
✗ not found: <server detail>
The server’s own wording is passed through, because that is what separates “not in the pool” from “not your lead”.
400
✗ rejected: <server detail>
Followed by the two usual causes: a cursor reused after a re-sort, or a convert on a lead with no revealed address.
401 / 403
✗ not authorized — run `vxcli auth login`
Expired or missing credential.
other
✗ <action> failed (HTTP <code>): <detail>
Falls back to no detail returned when the body carries none.
Three of these were exercised directly::

$ vxcli --no-color salesshift leads show 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000

exit 1

✗ rejected: Malformed cursor
    Usual causes       a cursor reused after changing the sort or filters,
                       or a convert on a lead with no revealed address
exit 1

$ HOME=/tmp/empty vxcli --no-color salesshift leads quota
✗ quota: not authenticated — run `vxcli auth login` first
exit 1

$ HOME=/tmp/empty vxcli --no-color salesshift stats
✗ stats failed (HTTP 0): not authenticated — run `vxcli auth login` first
exit 1
```

The command to run after something came back 402 Payment Required.
It shows the resolved plan, who runs the compute, the sending and the model, and every allowance. A null allowance is unlimited.
On Self-Hosted, emails and AI are not an allowance of zero — they are not ours to meter, because the mail leaves your mailbox over your IP and the model call bills to your key. The managed flags are what say so, and this command prints them rather than the misleading number.

The node a self-hosted workspace runs itself
On Self-Hosted the tenant's own vxnode does the sending, the crawling and the agent work that we do for paid plans.
Registration is a handshake, not a text field: the control plane calls the node's /health and requires it to report this workspace's tenant id before the host is written down. Run with no subcommand to see the current state.

Clears the host, the verification time and the fingerprint. Sending, crawling and agent work stop until another node is registered — nothing falls back to our infrastructure, because on this plan it never ran there.

Verify email addresses — live mailbox check with an explainable verdict

Verify email addresses — live mailbox check with an explainable verdict
Verify email addresses with the SalesShift Lead Verifier.
Each address goes through syntax, domain, MX, provider, disposable/role, SPF/DMARC, a live SMTP dialogue with the mail server, and a catch-all test. Every check prints as it finishes, then the verdict (verified, risky, not_verified or inconclusive), a 0-100 score with an A-F grade, and the reasons behind it. The probe stops at RCPT TO: no email is ever sent.
Limits: 12 checks per user per minute, 150 per workspace per hour. Runs of more than one address are paced about 5 s apart to stay inside the per-minute window; --file reads at most 150 addresses.
Exit codes: 0 every address is verified or risky 1 none would bounce, but at least one is inconclusive 2 at least one address is not_verified (mail would bounce) 3 a check could not be run (auth, rate limit, network, bad input)

heading_path: What was and was not run
chunks.text:
The groups documented in prose above were executed against a live system and their output pasted verbatim. On 2026-08-12 a second pass ran the CRM, automation and signal groups against https://api.vxcloud.io : tasks create/update/complete/delete, workflow validate, test-run and enroll, a sequence taken from create through step, activate, enroll, analytics and pause, and an opportunity applied to — which recorded the application and delivered a real email, with a second apply correctly refused 409 .
That pass found nine defects, three of which were the dangerous kind that returns a plausible number rather than an error: a multi-word --q was not percent-encoded and answered 400 ; contact search matched column by column, so "Joel" and "Wembo" each found people but "Joel Wembo" found none; and sequence analytics read its counters one level above where they live, reporting 0 sent for a sequence that had really sent eight. All nine are fixed and re-verified.
On 2026-08-13 the free-tier additions to billing were run against http://localhost:8741 : entitlements in both renderings, node , and two of the three node register refusals. The commands that change what a workspace is paying, or stop it sending, were not.
The exceptions below were never run, for the reasons given.
Command
Status
Why
leads erasure
not run
Global and irreversible across every tenant, against a real person. Only its --email guard was exercised. Everything else about it on this page is read from the source and labelled as such.
billing activate
not run
The workspace these captures come from is a comped Organization. Activating a free plan would have taken that away, and the command’s own refusal rules mean it could not simply be undone.
billing node detach
not run
There was no node registered to detach, and detaching a real one stops that tenant sending until another is registered.
billing node register <host>
refusals only

heading_path: What was and was not run
chunks.text:
All three refusal paths — 403, 400 and 502 — were run live, and none of them wrote anything. A successful registration was not: it needs a node whose /health answers with this workspace’s tenant id, and repointing a live sending workspace at one is not a thing to do for a screenshot.
Three commands were run in a mode that deliberately avoids a side effect, and the page says which mode: convert-from-pool with --no-reveal (spent nothing, created nothing), bulk-convert against one already-converted and one unrevealed lead (converted nothing new), and enrich against a company already in the pool (added nothing). One reveal and one conversion were genuinely spent, and one real email was sent, so that those three could be shown working rather than described.

chunks.text:
These are not gaps in one language. No SalesShift SDK, in any language, has a method for any of them. Use the REST API directly.
- Companies, deals, pipelines and forecast
- Quotes, products, and the invoices you send customers
- Contracts and e-signature
- Calendar, events and ICS invitations
- Customer subscriptions, MRR, reports, dashboards and goals
- Deliverability and the sending pool
- Marketing — forms, landing pages, booking links, automations
- Webmail — accounts, OAuth connect, message sync
- Settings, team and provider webhooks
- Reply threads — the whole /conversations area
- AI email drafting (/ai/write-email)
- All 55 messaging and call routes (51 HTTP, 4 WebSocket)
Three flows people expect to find here, and do not
Fetch deliverability health — no SDK reaches the deliverability or sending-pool routes. The nearest thing any of them has is the tenant node’s email-worker health check, which reports the worker’s providers and rate limit, not domain authentication or inbox placement.
Read what came back — there is no method for /conversations in any language. An SDK can send, and can list sent mail with its engagement counters, but the reply threads themselves are REST only.
Do any of this from the Python async client — vxsdk_async.py has a SalesShift resource, and it covers email and the leads pool and stops there. It has no billing method at all, new or old, and none of the CRM, workflow or sequence surface the sync client gained. Every count on this page for “Python” is the sync client.

chunks.page_title: Go, Python, TypeScript, C++ and Java SDKs
chunks.text:
Every SDK accepts the same two credentials the API does: a JWT access token, or a developer API key ( xc_dev_ , xc_test_ , xc_live_ ). Go, Python and TypeScript can also read whatever vxcli auth login already stored in ~/.vxcloud/credentials.json , which is how every example on this page authenticates. C++ and Java have no such loader — pass the credential yourself.
Language
From vxcli's credentials
Explicit
Go
vxsdk.LoadFromVxcli(ctx, opts...)
vxsdk.New(ctx, vxsdk.WithJWT(a, r))
Python
vxsdk.Client.load_from_vxcli()
vxsdk.Client(access_token=…)
TypeScript
VxCloud.loadFromVxcli(opts?)
new VxCloud( { accessToken } )
C++
none
vx::ClientOptions { .access_token = … }
Java
none
VxClient.builder().accessToken(…)
Only the API-key path refreshes: the Go, Python, TypeScript, C++ and Java clients all exchange a key for a JWT on demand and retry once on a 401. A client constructed from a bare JWT has nothing to refresh with, so an expired token surfaces as a 401 for you to handle.

A client cannot infer what a workspace may do from what it is paying: a trial has a clock on it, an allowance runs out mid-month, and a capability pointed at the tenant’s own account is not metered at all. Three clients have methods for asking. They are the first thing to reach for when a call comes back 402 Payment Required , which is what every plan refusal looks like — never a 403.
Operation
Go
Python (sync)
TypeScript
Resolved plan, managed flags and allowances
GetEntitlements(ctx)
billing_entitlements()
entitlements()
Move onto a free plan
ActivatePlan(ctx, code)

activatePlan(planCode)
Node state and the id it must claim
GetSelfHosted(ctx)
billing_self_hosted()
selfHosted()
Register a node
RegisterNode(ctx, host)
billing_register_node(host)
registerNode(host)
Forget it again
DetachNode(ctx)

heading_path: Registering a node is a handshake
chunks.text:
registerNode does not store what you pass it. The control plane fetches <host>/health and requires the node to report this workspace’s tenant id before the host is written down; a node that names a different workspace is refused. HTTPS is required except for localhost . All three clients surface the server’s own wording rather than inventing their own.
```
# Go
salesshift.RegisterNode: salesshift.RegisterNode: 400 Bad Request — {"detail":"The node must be reachable over HTTPS."}

# Python
VxValidationError -> salesshift.billing_register_node: 400 Bad Request — {"detail":"The node must be reachable over HTTPS."}

# TypeScript
VxValidationError -> The node must be reachable over HTTPS.
```
Python and TypeScript also refuse an empty host before making a request at all — salesshift.billing_register_node: host is required — which matches how billing_checkout guards its own argument.
The doubled prefix in the Go line is real
Nothing here was activated or registered
